subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECTS OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext: What a stupid statement! It could only come from you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECTS OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
I knew once I got on my feet that I would liven up this debate. My good friend, the Conservative whip, and I have an ongoing relationship of shouting back and forth. Without being overly partisan, I believe that we should look behind some of the so-called logic we have seen in the speeches last night, this morning, and this afternoon.
1 should like to deal with the substance of the motion and the whole question of the economy. Of course high interest rates are troubling us. One option outlined by the Minister of Finance was to allow the Canadian dollar to slide even further. 1 think the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada have done excellent jobs in trying to steer that balance, to ensure that the dollar does not fall, to ensure that we do not open up the floodgates to rampant inflation, and also to ensure that high interest rates do not get out of control.
I think the Minister of Finance made a very salient point in criticizing the interest rate policies of the United States in the last few weeks. 1 do not know whether it is because there is a lame duck administration in the United States. Perhaps the President of the United States is not undertaking the usual
Economic Conditions
direction as he should in the period leading up to January 20. Perhaps Mr. Miller, or whoever is running the Federal Reserve Board, is running the whole country. I would submit that the high interest rate policies now being pursued by the United States are very likely, or could very likely if they continue, plunge the whole world economy into a severe recession, perhaps even a depression.
Last night the Minister of Finance outlined that Canada cannot divorce itself from the economic realities in the United States. In a sense, we are a passenger in that vehicle, the vehicle being the United States, in its ride to high interest rates. There is a school of economics in the United States, the Monetary school, or the school of Mr. Friedman, the Chicago school, which believes this is what we need. Some of the things I have heard in speeches from members opposite remind me of comments 1 have heard in my constituency made by my opponents from time to time. They say that what this country needs is a good shake-out, a good recession, a good depression and we will get back to honest, old-fashioned values.
If you look back over the last 50 years, perhaps even longer, you will see that the Conservative party philosophy is based on the assumption that the state should not intervene in the economy, that the people should tough it out. There is no compassion, in the policies of that party. We saw it in the depression years of the 1930s, and, as a result, the Conservative party has paid for that over the last 50 years by not being in power in this country. They are seen as the party which does not care.
Quite frankly, I find it personally offensive that the Leader of the Opposition lectured us yesterday on the effects of our economic policies on lower-income Canadians, when his party has an historic record of putting it quite strongly to the disadvantaged groups of Canadians. These groups are comprised of the lower-income people, pensioners and so on. One has only to look at the budget which was presented a year ago by the former minister of finance to see how Conservative economic policies take their greatest toll against those who can least afford to pay their way in society and those who can least protect themselves-the poor, the disadvantaged, the minorities, and pensioners.
I know the Leader of the Opposition has an affinity for the policies of Mrs. Margaret Thatcher in England. 1 am thankful that the election in May, 1979, did not produce a majority government for the other side, because people in Great Britain right now would just have loved to have had the opportunity that we had last December in voting out the government when its old-fashioned, right wing economic policy is shown to fail. Unfortunately, the people in Great Britain do not have the option which we had last year in kicking out the goverment. As a result, that great country-the country where I was born, incidentally-will go through probably the worst crisis it has ever had since the twenties, the general strike of 1926, and the depression. My parents and grandparents went through that and it was Tory governments which were in power at that time

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
under Mr. Baldwin, which forced the people of Great Britain into dire economic straits. We see this happening now in Great Britain. I am only bringing it up because I am very glad and relieved that Canadian people had a chance to pronounce upon the economic policies of the former government, unlike the people of Great Britain, who now must basically put up with Mrs. Thatcher for the next few years.
There are a few things which I would really like to deal with in a general way. It is all tied in with the economic debate and the energy debate. I think all of us on this side, and my colleague from Willowdale, put it very succinctly this morning, are concerned with what is happening in western Canada. We are concerned about the so-called alienation and the so-called discontent. I think all of us on this side of Elouse are reasonable people. I think the government will be reasonable in any future negotiations it has with the other provinces.
But what 1 see happening, aside from the historical, legitimate grievances of western Canadians, and the historical antipathy to our party, some of it perhaps being warranted, from statements made or actions taken in the past, is that we have basically a philosophical debate, which is quite legitimate. That is what politics is all about in a democray. But, unfortunately, it is being masked by members on the other side by the cloth of separatist feelings in western Canada, of western alienation. I find it offensive.
When you listen to the argument which member on the other side advance against Bill C-48 and other aspects of Canadianizing our oil and gas industry, obviously it is their legitimate right to disagree with the philosophy of this party and this government, which is to ask for a mandate to increase Canadian ownership of our oil and gas industry, but some hon. members call this socialism. 1 do not call it that. When the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) sets out in this country and talks about nationalizing every single oil company, that is socialism in its pure sense. All we are talking about, Mr. Speaker, is Canadianizing the industry.
What I find offensive is that the members opposite in the Tory party, many of them western Canadians, are playing up the historical grievances, in effect whipping up this spirit, this sentiment, this fear. What they are really doing is using western alienation and western frustrations as a vehicle for their own philosophical argument against the government for its Canadianization policy toward the oil industry, and its policy to keep lower energy prices.
It is true that Sheik Yamani, for example, has talked about an $80 per barrel price for oil this time next year. Members on the other side feel we, in this country, should move in a knee-jerk way to every single increase by OPEC when we have the security of supply here, where we can perhaps cushion the blows which Canadians might otherwise have had to suffer because of the adverse economic situations brought on by higher oil and gas prices.

speechtext:
I see members are heckling me over there. One thing that worries me is that a lot of them are so
exacerbated by the political debate and their own rhetoric that they are denying us the democratic right which they claim we are only trying to tear down. 1 find it quite ironic, and it is quite a tale being told here this afternoon, that we have a great element of democracy, since we have had this emergency debate requested by the two opposition parties. It has gone on all night and is now into the twentieth hour-twenty-second hour-whatever it is. I do not know when it will end, perhaps tomorrow or Sunday. But this is a great exercise in democracy. Every single member of this Elouse has the right to stand here and propound and talk about the economic and national problems which concern them.
I find it a bit ironic-supreme irony, as some people would say-that members opposite who object to our constitutional and economic policies have heckled me, as the Leader of the Opposition heckled the Minister of Finance last night through most of our speeches. That is not what democracy is all about. We have legitimate views to express. I have tried to be fair and mild this afternoon, but I think the game which is being played by members in the Conservative party, especially those from western Canada, is a very dangerous game. It is an extremely dangerous game. They are trying to turn people in the west against all other forms of political expression, whether it be through the NDP or the Liberals.
I have had an ongoing dialogue with the hon. member from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who is a former Speaker of this House. He sent me some editorials from the Edmonton Journal criticizing the policies of our government. 1 wrote back to him and asked him to look at editorials in The Calgary Herald. I told him those editorials had been a bit more objective. They did not agree with us lock, stock and barrel, but they were somewhat objective and basically favourable to the constitutional proposals. And he is trying to argue the opposite. This has taken place in our personal correspondence which we have been exchanging.
What offends me about some of the statements made by people on the other side is that they will brook no opposition. They are so self-righteous that they believe we in the government are destroying the country. Really, what we are doing is asking Canadians to make some basic choices. We are asking them to make the basic choice as to the kind of confederation they want to live in, whether they want to live in a confederation of ten semi-autonomous loosely knit states where certain provinces have the ability to use their economic powers to the detriment of the rest of the country, or whether they want to live in a country where there is an overriding national interest which recognizes the rights of all Canadians to share in each other's fortune and misfortune.
That is the kind of country for which we have been arguing over the past couple of years, and that is what underlines our constitutional reform proposal. We feel strongly that the provinces, particularly those in the west, must have the lion's share of the wealth derived from oil and gas. That is right, because it
December 19, 1980

is in the British North America Act that the provinces do own these resources.
There must be an element of sharing. We cannot permit one economy or one region of the country to become so powerful that in effect it becomes a countervailing power against the federal government which represents the national interest. That is really what the debate is about. 1 am sorry my friends opposite are not willing to listen to the arguments that have been put forward.
There are legitimate fears in western Canada over the issue of resource ownership. I should say that in the constitutional resolution now before the committee, the government did not alter in any way the provisions of the existing BNA Act as they deal with resources. In fact the Prime Minister, along with the government, has agreed to suggestions made by the NDP which, while they do not agree with us all the time, are at least working to improve the constitutional package. The government has agreed to make certain changes so that the security of resources is guaranteed to the provinces, in particular to those in the west, in any new constitution.
There are also some changes on indirect taxation, and the entrenchment of that principle as I understand it. That will be an improvement. If members opposite want some other kind of guarantees that resource ownership will always accrue to the provinces, the government would be amenable. I have not heard anything contrary on our side. I have not heard anything to suggest that the federal Parliament wants to take over the resources of the provinces.
There is a question about offshore resources but that is a legitimate constitutional question. The problem is that members opposite have set up their own straw men and are trying to knock them down all over the country. Their arguments are straw men. You can always make your own supposition, which may not be true, and go around the country trying to defend it, or you can attribute arguments to your opponent and then go around the country trying to knock down your opponent's argument when, in reality, the opponent has not made those arguments.
I believe there has been a very great distortion. The debate recently, both inside and outside the House, has been unCanadian. We have the forum of the House of Commons within which we can express our views. I have drawn repeated attention to the hysterical reaction of some of the members opposite. There is one view over there and there is another view here, and that is what democracy is all about. In the election of last February, Canadians chose to return to office a party which, over the years, has given good government, efficient government, and compassionate government. It is a government which has been tolerant of all regions and all points of view in this country.
The electorate rejected a government which sought by its economic policies and its budget to squeeze the small individual in society and to hurt groups which are least able to defend themselves. That is democracy. 1 agree with what the Minister of Finance said here last night. There is an element of bitterness in the points of view being expressed by members of the
Economic Conditions
official opposition which transcends their legitimate concern over the legitimate economic problems we face in Canada today.
1 see that my time has expired. I have made these comments in the best of faith, and I am only sorry that members of the official opposition cannot accept that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for several weeks 1 have looked forward to speaking on the crisis which faces the economy of this country and which has been brought on by the socialist rhetoric we just heard from the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette). I am from Ontario and I am ashamed that that gentleman is from the same province. 1 am ashamed of many of the politicians from Ontario. They are trying to retain the west in a slave situation as they have always done. They could charge them what they would.
We have heard various descriptions of the government over the last 23 hours in this chamber, but one which 1 heard from the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan)

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
about the nursery rhyme "Wynken, Blynken and Nod" appealed to me. I think that the present government is creating a new nursery story, "Quacky Mac, Miserable Marc and their PET". Fortunately, citizens of this country have benefited from the great resources with which they are blessed. Since our inception we have enjoyed the plentiful production of agriculture. We have had great woods and forests to produce lumber and pulp and paper. We have had a plentiful supply of water for hydro power and for other purposes. Our minerals are second to none and our hydrocarbons are now becoming of great importance.
Because of this, we have not had to become an industrial nation. We have not had to keep up to the requirements of other members of OECD. The Liberal government over the past 12 years has shunned the potential of this country to become a major industrial nation. Instead, it has concentrated on destroying the Canadian work ethic and the Canadian wish to save money and invest in this country, and this has created a disastrous condition.
The youth of this country will be burdened for the unforeseeable future with double-digit inflation, a valueless dollar, and a debt burden beyond the wildest dreams of Lord Keynes. This same government has done nothing to develop the industrial base of the country. The same government is determined to destroy the only base we have, which is our natural resources. It has removed the opportunity of self-sufficiency by 1990 with their program of nationalism for the oil industry.
This program does not affect the Seven Sisters or the large multinationals. They do not have to worry because they know it is for a period of time. They have oil in the ground. They have the wealth there. They do not need to take it out now because, if they leave it in the ground, it will be brought out later at a much higher price. Some day soon the Canadian public will wake up cold. Some morning they will decide that it is time to turf out the Liberal government which has been disastrous for this country over the last 12 years.
We must keep in mind why the multinationals are not terribly concerned with the government's energy program. Their warehousing costs on their inventory are zero which means no increased price. What I am concerned about is what it does to our junior and senior Canadian oil development companies. They keep talking about the 10 per cent and 35 per cent kickbacks. That is fine if there is any cash flow for a kickback. But the government must remember those companies have to come up with 65 per cent of the money. If the Canadian investment community is not prepared to bring that money in, then they must depend on a cash flow which has been totally eroded by provincial taxes, and now excessive federal tax.
This group of Canadian companies, fortunately for many Canadians shareholders, was aware of this situation last spring as soon as the election came. They started raising funds in Canada from Canadians to subsidize their subsidiaries in the United States. Those corporations which started in the last
year are successful in the United States because they have freedom to make money and to create a cash flow which will in turn help the United States to become self-sufficient more quickly than we ever could.
The only money left in Canada from the oil producing companies is the little bit left over after governments have taken their big slice. Why would an oil company work in this climate? In Canada they are lucky to get $6.20 net per barrel. In England, which has been related to us as an example, their take is said to be 51 per cent. A junior Canadian oil company would much rather have 49 per cent of a $40 barrel than 33 per cent of a $17 barrel.
In the U.S. they keep 73 per cent of the $40 barrel. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) many times in the past week or two has mentioned that the rigs are not moving out of Canada. Maybe they are not right now. Maybe this side has overstated how many rigs are moving out at present. But many of the rigs, prior to this budget, were committed to contract. They cannot close down when they have gone down 1,000 feet and have 14,000 feet to go. These companies were committed to a contract. The effect of that budget has not hit us yet. We have not felt it to the degree we will by the end of 1981.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) refers to all of the money which will be available for investment in Canada. The minister should go to Dallas and Houston and start talking to some of the bankers down there. Many of those banks, even with the new Bank Act, are not setting up in Canada. They do not have to. Canadians have gone to them. There is not point in them setting up in Canada because the money is flowing down there. That is another factor which is affecting the devalued price of our dollar.
I wish the government would find out where our capital is going and what is happening to it. The wealth of this country is fleeing. It is not fleeing in the hundreds, thousands or millions, it is fleeing in the billions. Every week we can see in magazines new buildings being put up in every city throughout the United States, exemplary of where our money is going.
1 believe it is time for the government to realize the errors of its ways. It is not too late now; it may be later. I realize that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is intractable. He will not change. But I plead with the Prime Minister of the country to make a change and get somebody who knows something about the conditions of the oil business in this country.
The billions of dollars 1 refer to are fleeing because of the free spending, bureaucratic-riddled, Liberal government with socialistic views. If you want an eyeful, read the government's working paper on capital gains. Its proposals will again erode the capital base in Canada.
I plead with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, whoever it may be, to take the tax off those low-income people who have to heat their homes and put it on transportation. If that were done, that would reduce the turnover period of a car from ten years back to seven years. General Motors is not selling small fuel-efficiency cars today. General Motors is
December 19, 1980

selling all its big Chevs and Oldsmobile. If the tax were put on transportation, people would stop buying big cars. Things would be more efficient because more people would travel in a car together at the same time.
Now we come to the question of interest rates, which is a very interesting situation. People on both sides of the House disagree on what we should do. There is one scenario that has never been approached nor tested. We are living in a rollercoaster age of interest rates. It forces many Canadians, both individuals and corporate structures, into bankruptcy. I give you an example; the CMHC and the AHOP program. The government started this program. Houses were sold. People could not afford them nor could they keep them up. These houses come back on the market and are sold at lower prices than they were in the first place. Prospective buyers for these houses which have come on the market will be able, as of January 10, to get a 2 per cent lower mortgage rate than they originally had when these houses were sold. If the government is going to give something to some people, it must do it for all. I say to the government, let us not be selective just so as to unload an asset which it is unable to sell.
1 want to speak about this roller-coaster ride. Instead of the interest rates going up and down and knocking people and businesses out of business, what about letting our dollar be a roller coaster? Does the government realize that, if that happens, people in Canada would stop buying large ticket items? They could not afford them. A $25,000 Cadillac would become a $50,000 Cadillac. People would think twice. This would encourage Canadians to create more, and so help our industrial base. It would also protect those people with homes. It would enable them to keep their homes. It would protect industry and assist industry to become bigger and better. I say we should try that now.
We have tried everything else and we have failed with everything else. We would go up and we would go down. In March we could be up and in August we could be down. In November we could be up, but when would we be down again? My guess is that this time the government will leave the high interest rate on two months instead of one month and then it will go zapping down again.
It is the low-income Canadian about whom I am concerned. It is also the middle-income Canadian who has been hammered by every government we have in the country, municipal, regional, provincial, federal-you name it, they all have their hands in the middle-income pocket. It is time we got out of the pockets of the middle-income people. It is time we gave them a break with their mortgages so these people can own their own homes. It is time we gave them mortgage deductibility as we had proposed. It is time to give Canadians a break, not only the low income Canadians but others as well.
I happen to have given my colleagues an article written by Louis Ruckeyser. It was published in the Houston Chronicle. I just want to make the record clear. He did not say "Thank you Canada". He said, "Thank you again Canada". Thank you for last year giving our hostages back. Thank you this year for bringing billions of dollars into our country".
Economic Conditions
Many people have spoken in this debate, and I can go on and on. It is not hard to get any new material because we know the disaster which is existing today in Canada's economy. We know what is happening to industry in Ontario. We know what is happening to the drilling operations out west. We know that it is hitting the service industry. I can go on with what everyone else has said, but I just want to conclude by saying that we are heading on a one-way ride to hell in a handcart because we will not have the fuels to get us there by conventional means.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened rather carefully to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette), especially his comments or view that he thought that British people would love the opportunity to turf out the Thatcher government. I would like to assure the hon. member there are an increasing number of Canadians who would love the opportunity to turf out this government, based on its economic policies. I would like to substantiate that by reading a few lines of letters I have received from constituents. I assume other members in this House can probably repeat much the same kind of comments that they have been receiving.
The first is from an unemployed Canadian who states, "It seems to me that the Trudeau government doesn't care about Canadians being out of work". The next is from a senior citizen, "Look into the high price of milk and bread." Another says, "I am one of the victims of a recent lay-off from a foreign-owned company. 1 would suggest more measures be introduced for the purpose of protecting such employees. I've worked for this company for six years, but still I have to go."
Another constituent wrote, "Conditions in this country stink. Big companies never pay any taxes-that's why the working people are so poor. Look at the price of food. Who's making the big money? The companies come to this country and bleed it dry. They do nothing for veterans."
The last one is, "The Canadian economy has gone to hell." I think an increasing number of Canadians would agree with those sentiments.
I am glad that finally the members of this House have been given an opportunity to discuss the economic crisis we are faced with in Canada today. It is a crisis that has been in existence for some period of time and this discussion finally came about as a result of yesterday's announcement that the increase in the cost of living for the month of November was at its highest since March of 1975, and yesterday's increase in interest rates broke through all previous high records.
To date the government has not presented one proposal to deal with this crisis, to present proposals that would alleviate the hardships that the government's fiscal policies are inflicting on the senior citizens of our country and on others on fixed incomes, on small businesses in Canada which are being pushed to the wall by the government's interest rate policies, on those Canadians who are faced with mortgages coming up

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
for renewal, or those Canadians who had dreamed of buying a home and whose dream will not be realized.
In addition to those problems we also have the economic and social costs of having over a million Canadians unemployed, and that figure is growing at a frightening rate every day.
The response of the government to date has been to blame this crisis on everyone else and it has refused to accept the responsibility which is its to deal with those problems. However, the government was not so apparently unconcerned when its members sat as the official opposition last year, in 1979.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), then leader of the opposition, on October 29, as reported in Hansard, asked this question of the then prime minister:
Since, in the view of the government, we have to follow American interest rates up to I 1 per cent, 12 per cent, 13 per cent, 14 per cent, at what rate do we begin to look at alternatives? I just remind the Prime Minister that at his press conference on Friday he said, "Given the situation that we face in the economy now, we literally have no alternative except alternatives that will make the situation worse in times to come." At what point will the government look at these alternatives, rather than following the American interest rate up to 13 per cent, 14 per cent and God knows how high?
Later in the same day the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) had this to say:
This evening I want to speak particularly about interest rates because they are not in fact something that is remote from the daily lives of Canadians. Interest rates are costs and costs are part of prices. They affect everything done by Canadians and their families. The present record level of interest rates which is supported by Conservative policy cuts back the ability of Canadians to buy goods and services of all kinds, such as cars, homes, food and clothing, everything people need. Those high interest rates cut back on the ability of factories and businesses generally to expand, to create more production and jobs.
These high interest rates limit the ability of business, especially small business, simply to operate on basic non-inflationary levels. Therefore, these high interest rates mean losses of production and jobs now and over the coming winter months. The Conservative government has been saying that these high interest rates are needed to fight inflation but they in themselves drive up costs and add to inflation.
The Liberal party, which at least pretends to be the champion of working people while in opposition, is obviously no such champion once it forms the government.
This government agreed a year ago with the arguments presented by members of my party on the effects of high interest rate policies. I can also quote many such other statements made by government members when they sat in opposition and were then horrified at our unemployment levels. Nowhere is that problem more apparent than in the number of young people we have in Canada who are unemployed and the unacceptably high levels of unemployment among women in our country.
The steady deterioration of the position of women in the labour force is a cause for grave concern. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) gave what has become his standard reply, in response to my question on November 5 regarding employment training opportunities for women. Superficial incentives, ineffective programs, and yet more waiting for the results of yet more studies was his reply.
The position of women in the labour force has been studied to death and, if the figures change at all, it is only to show that
the situation is getting worse. Women continue to be overrepresented in the unemployment figures and underrepresented in high ranking, high paying positions.
Women experience higher unemployment than men in every industry except construction. In 1979 the unemployment rate for married women was 95 per cent higher than the rate for married men. Re-entry women comprised the largest component of the female unemployed. Most of these women who are unemployed could benefit from training programs which would provide them with skills to ensure them a good paying job with opportunities for advancement.
The problem is that those women who do find work have an eight in ten chance of winding up in a traditional occupation, such as clerical, sales, technical or service. Even there, with over one and a half million more women working now than ten years ago, the distribution of women in the work force has remained the same. There are simply more women doing the same types of jobs.
As a result of the segregation of women into low-paying, low-skilled, dead-end jobs, the wage gap continues to increase. Today, for every dollar a man earns, a woman earns 58 cents.
Study after study simply reconfirms those appalling facts, and study after study shows that the situation is getting worse, not better. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has both the responsibility and the resources to guarantee women an equal position in the labour force. Is his lack of concrete action an indication of a lack of commitment? 1 rather suspect that to be the case.
A recent report by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women which studied federal employment programs showed that these programs consistently favoured men at the expense of women, that women were underrepresented in all direct job-creation programs except two programs for youth and that women received lower wages than men under government wage-subsidy programs. The minister's recent announcement of more programs will just perpetuate the inequity which already exists. We do not need more money spent to foster more inequality. We need adequate funding for well-thought-out programs which will achieve the proper objective: good paying, long-term jobs for women.
The employment training programs which currently exist need reassessment as well. The programs are not concluding with the desired results. In 1978-79 only 33 per cent of all full-time trainees in the institutional programs were women. Only 29 per cent of all industrial trainees were women. More than 50 per cent of these women were being trained for stenographic, typing, and other clerical jobs. It is no small irony that women begin their occupational segregation in Canada Manpower employment training programs.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration has announced increased incentives to employers to hire women in non-traditional jobs. In 1978, 75 per cent of those subsidies went to small, non-union firms with 20 or fewer employees. By channelling female trainees into small firms the trainees run
December 19, 1980

the risk of becoming a cheap source of labour and vulnerable to lay-offs and unemployment. In 1975, three months after women completed their training in a non-traditional occupation, it was found that they earned $67 less than men with identical characteristics in similar occupations. Because the department only does a limited three-month follow-up of its trainees, it is difficult to determine if women are retained as permanent employees in any significant numbers.
Another problem with the subsidy program is that it is limited to areas where women's participation is 10 per cent or less. This narrow definition of non-traditional jobs increases the likelihood of failure by women since it places huge responsibilities on a few women to prove success, and guarantees that they will experience tremendous isolation.
The affirmative action program the minister keeps offering as a panacea is short-sighted and superficial. First of all, it has been implemented in only three of the approximately 100 federal departments and agencies. Second, a close look at the program shows that in reality what has been implemented is really not an affirmative action program but just another study of the discrimination that women in these three departments face in relation to hiring and promotion. If the federal government is seriously committed to equality for women in the labour force, it should implement a hard affirmative action policy in the federal public service to set an example for private industry. Further, it should use the clout it has in $11 billion worth of business in contracts purchased from private companies. Contract compliance has been highly successful in the United States. Under this policy initiative, women and minorities have found that, for the first time, they have had access to jobs and training previously inaccessible to them.
"Limited success", "a dismal record", and "far too little progress" is how the minister himself recently described the employment training programs for women. I hope the minister will, in the immediate future, use the vast resources available to him to change the deplorable situation women in the labour force now find themselves facing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate was ordered on the basis that there is a serious economic crisis in the country requiring, as Standing Order 26 points out, urgent consideration. Those words "crisis" and "urgent consideration", which were used by Madam Speaker in granting this debate have, of course, been pooh-poohed and rejected outright by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Yet, if anything is indicative of the fact that hon. members in the opposition parties consider that the economic situation in Canada today is of crisis proportions, surely that indicator is this debate in which we are engaged, because it is unprecedented, at least in recent years. I probably would have to check with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to see just how far back it was that we had a continuous debate of this length, but I have a feeling it is well back into the early part of the century.
What we have is a debate which has been going on for some 19 to 20 hours, and nothing which has transpired in this
Economic Conditions
country in the last ten, 15 or 20 years has triggered a continuous debate of this nature.
When we look at the events which did transpire here in Canada in those years, and when we think of depressions, recessions, international conflicts and internal tensions, and realize that none of them prompted a debate of this nature, we come to appreciate the seriousness and the gravity of the economic situation which triggered this discussion session.
Members of the Conservative party and of the New Democratic Party are concerned, and deeply concerned, about the effects of galloping inflation, the devalued dollar we have to contend with, high interest rates and escalating costs of food, home heating fuels, and housing. The prices of all these things are going up. These costs affect ordinary Canadians up and down the country, especially Canadians on lower incomes, and particularly the one million unemployed. Yes, we are concerned about it. The tragedy is that members of Parliament on the government benches, whether they happen to be backbenchers or ministers of the Crown, those people in the House who really could take some action to alleviate this situation, do not seem to be the least bit concerned about it. Liberal member after Liberal member has risen in this debate to defend the government's economic policies which, I say, can only be described as hard-hearted, cruel, and insensitive. That is what they are at this point.
A Liberal member opposite shakes his head. 1 realize that he does not feel that way. None of the Liberal members do, and that is the difficulty. The problem is that the government is totally insensitive to the economic woes of the country today. I suppose the more charitable description which could be applied to the point of view of hon. members opposite is that they are misguided, but this is not a time when the country can put up with a government which has views which are misguided.
At a time like this, with the highest interest rates in the country's history and with one of the highest year-over-year increases in the cost of living, the Minister of Finance is floundering around like a fish out of water. He will castigate anyone in sight for the ills of the country, anyone, that is, but the Liberal government, which is the author of our misfortunes. He and his colleagues, for instance, blame the government of the United States, and after what the minister has had to say about the policies of our neighbours to the south, is it any wonder that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is reluctant to accept the invitation of President-elect Reagan to go to Washington? Is it any wonder? Yes, the Minister of Finance will blame the Americans, he will blame the international situation, he will blame the provinces, and he will blame the oil and gas industry. I suppose the next thing he will do is blame the weather. He will try to emulate one of his predecessor Liberal ministers of finance.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext: John Turner.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
The minister's only policy, it seems to me, in the absence of government policy, is to go on the offensive and to try to find a scapegoat. Well, that is simply

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
not good enough for a government which has been in power, this time for ten months, and previous to that for ten to 15 years without coming up with a responsible set of economic policies to offer to the Canadian public.
There are things the Canadian government can do. Ministers cannot just sit there, throw up their hands and say, "It is not our business, it is all because of what the Americans are doing, or what the U.S. government is doing." They owe the Canadian public more than that, and there are things that the government can be doing.
1 want to mention just a couple of areas where the government should be moving now before it causes any more difficulty, any more hardship, and any more suffering to thousands of Canadians up and down this land, where it could reverse policies that have already been taken, or where it could initiate new policies which could perhaps be helpful. The two areas I want to mention are indexing and energy policy. I realize that they have been touched on before, but 1 want to mention them again because the Minister of Finance has made a great to-do in the last few days about the fact that those on fixed incomes, such as pensioners, have their monthly cheques indexed to the increases in the cost of living. This indexing, he protests, should be able to take care of all their concerns, all their additional costs. He says they should not have any worries. Well, he knows how false that is and he knows that it does not meet the situation.
What the minister cannot or will not understand is that indexing for pensioners is based on the cost increases of all items right across the board, many of which are considered luxury items and certainly non-essential items to people in the low-income bracket. The cost of these non-essential items does not rise as fast as the necessities of life. The difference between the two categories is quite marked. The cost of non-essentials goes up at a far less steeply increased rate than that of essentials. But since the non-essential goods and services play just as much a part in measuring the monthly increase in the cost of living, they therefore skewer the cost of living index and the rate at which it is applied to make it lower than it otherwise would be. Otherwise you would just be measuring the cost of essentials or necessary goods. This means that for those who spend the greater part of their incomes on essentials, on food, clothing and shelter, the cost of living increase is lower than it actually should be, and automatically, of course, so is the indexed additional payment that they receive.
Let me explain in specific detail what 1 mean so that even the Minister of Finance will understand. 1 take as an example a woman aged between 60 and 65 who received the spouse's allowance. She is widowed and unable to find work in the labour force because of her age. She has no other income than her monthly government cheque of some $350, and she has no way of supplementing that. There are many like her in Canada today. Her last monthly increase was $9.83 a month, based on a year-to-year increase of approximately 10 per cent in the
cost of living. But her living costs are centered on items which are escalating much more rapidly than 10 per cent a year.
She spends most of her limited income on food, clothing, and shelter. But the costs of food, clothing and shelter are escalating much more rapidly than 10 per cent a year, or even the 11.2 per cent figure which was reported yesterday. Food is going up at 15 per cent, likely to increase by 20 per cent next year. Home heating fuel is up by 26.9 per cent, clothing by 11 per cent, transportation, if she happens to own a car, is going up by 23 per cent. The $9.83 increase which she gets based on a 10 per cent cost of living increase, does not reflect the 15 per cent increase in her cost of food, the 26.9 per cent increase in her home heating costs, or the increase in her transportation costs. Yet all of her expenditure goes on these items.
Surely the minister can understand that all persons in this category cannot continue to pay the much higher prices for food, clothing, shelter and transportation, if the monthly adjustment they receive to offset inflation is not geared to the actual increases in the costs of the items on which they must spend their money if they are to survive in this economic crisis. Surely the government can instruct Statistics Canada to work out an index for the monthly adjustment to the incomes of pensioners, disabled, and those in the lower-income brackets, which will truly reflect their expenditures, which will make it more equitable for them. To be sure, this is only a minimal step, but it is one the minister could take to make the plight of those who are in the lower-income brackets, the plight of those who are most in need, a bit easier. That is one step that the government could take to ease the economic crisis for a great many people across this country today.
The second area that 1 want to mention has to do with the government's energy policy. In the budget, and in recent bills introduced in the House, we have been presented with an over-all energy program which daily has the effect of making Canada more and more dependent on increasing the importation of expensive offshore oil. Earlier this week, as we saw, the price of offshore oil to Canada went up by 10 per cent, by anywhere from $2 to $4 a barrel for imported crude. The OPEC countries, on which we are depending for some 420,000 barrels of oil a day, raised their selling price by 10 per cent and in so doing they added an additional half a billion dollars to Canada's international balance of payments deficit annually. There is no guarantee that that price of offshore oil will not go up again.
There is no guarantee that that price for oil, which has to be imported to eastern Canada if people in that part of the country are to have the fuel necessary to heat their homes and to drive their motor vehicles, will not take another jump, and. what is more, there is absolutely no sure and certain guarantee that these offshore oil supplies on which we are unfortunately dependent, will not be cut back and reduced at the whim of some other country. In other words, Canada is increasingly vulnerable to the vagaries of the world oil supply and world oil price, and will continue to be in that unhappy and unnecessary position so long as we do not have enough domestic production to supply our own oil needs.
December 19, 1980

Day after day we are reminded of the lack of security in offshore oil, of the lack of stability in offshore prices. Day after day we are reminded of the critical need for oil self-sufficiency in Canada. The federal government's every effort should be directed to reducing our dependence on offshore oil in the face of the dangers and costly struggles in the international oil scene. It should be directing every effort to achieving oil self-sufficiency for the country, and yet what have we seen in recent weeks and months?
We have seen the introduction of a national energy program which has done more to impede Canadian oil self-sufficiency than to promote it. Canadians certainly do not want to become, increasingly, hostages to international oil suppliers, but that is the direction in which the government is torcing the country to go. All too sadly the proof is there for anyone who wants to look at it, even the government.
The tar sands developments are stalled, oil rigs are drifting away, money available for energy investment is becoming tighter and, as a result of all those matters, Canada's production of oil will decline. That is the point the government must face. With that decline in domestic production we become increasingly dependent upon unstable, expensive, and unreliable supplies of foreign oil with all of the international pressures which that entails.
Earlier this year I spoke on this subject in the House. At that time 1 accused the government of allowing us to drift into a greater dependency on offshore oil. Now, thanks to the national energy program, I know that the government is directing us into greater dependency. Earlier this year the minister responded to my remarks about the energy crisis by rehashing the election campaign. That is not what I invited him to do. I pleaded with him at that time to consider Canada's situation in the face of increasing volatility in the oil-rich Middle East. Since then we have seen the outbreak of hostilities between Iran and Iraq, a conflict which dramatizes the instability of that part of the world. Of course, it accentuates the vulnerability of those countries such as Canada which are dependent, to some extent, upon that part of the world for their precious oil supplies.
Since the outbreak of the Iran-Iraq conflict, we have seen a reduction of some four million barrels per day in the supply of oil to industrialized countries. That is the amount to date, but there is nothing to say that it will not be reduced further in the future. Neither can we be sure that the conflict will not spread to neighbouring oil-producing countries.
Saudi Arabia, from which we buy 45 per cent of our offshore oil supplies, jumped its price to $38.50 per barrel earlier this week. But that is not the end of it. Sheik Yamani, that great friend of the Prime Minister, made a prediction earlier this week that the price of oil could hit $50 American per barrel by next spring, which is $59 per barrel Canadian. He said that the price of oil to dependent countries such as Canada could go up to $59 per barrel by next spring if the Iran-lraq conflict continues. He went on to say the following:
Economic Conditions
If the Gulf war carries on for much longer a mood of panic will develop on the markets, and if there are no reasonable reactions from western governments, then you'll get this price soon enough.
That is the situation into which the government's energy policy is directing us. At a time when the offshore price is going up, when offshore oil supplies are becoming much scarcer, when we have run through the surpluses because of the Iran-Iraq conflict, when we are more vulnerable to offshore situations, the government is making us more dependent upon foreign supplies rather than introducing policies which would increase domestic supplies. It is cutting back on our domestic supplies and forcing us to be hostages to international oil situations over which we have no control.
It has an effect for every single Canadian. I want to bring it down to the fact that these offshore international situations will reflect themselves in more unemployment in the country, higher cost for staples in the country, much greater difficulty for small businesses and many more bankruptcies. All of those things will happen.
I should like to finish my participation in this debate by reading a letter which I received from a I2-year-old child. I received this letter not long ago. It was written with all of a child's candour. It epitomizes the situation in which we find ourselves because of the lack of government policy. Her letter reads as follows:
My Dad has been unemployed for seven months. He has worked for a trust company for 18 years, and when the mortgage rates went up, he was assigned another job. Because of two health problems this seemed practically impossible, but still my Dad gave it a try, but couldn't handle these extra jobs. A little later he was laid off. . . We have gone without for these last few months and Mum says, "We're finding out who our real friends are". My Dad has taken a job delivering pizzas but still it isn't enough. We have gone through pain and suffering these past few months and nothing seems to go right . . . People can say they understand, but really they don't. You'll have to go through this to understand. If you can, please help us. I just decided to write. Well, thanks a lot for listening.
I ask the government to listen to what Canadians are saying all across the country, and it will learn soon enough that its policies must be changed.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but her allotted time has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I look at the clock I am reminded of the fact that this place has now been in continuous session for approximately 20 hours. I do not know if that is a record or not. Certainly it is a record over the 23-year period that I have been here.
It is interesting to reflect upon the fact that those hours are more time than we spent debating the constitution, the 59 government constitutional proposals, in the House. Also it is worth reflecting upon the fact that this special debate has been devoted almost exclusively, with one or two minor exceptions, to the economic situation in Canada today, to the economic crisis facing the country today.
I realize this means a particularly heavy burden on the support staff of this place, on the Hansard reporters and the

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
people who keep this institution going, but though what we have to say during the course of this debate may not be widely reported, it is important to remember that this debate is a signal to all across the country that we are in fact in the midst of a very serious and a very grave economic crisis.
The hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) said during the course of his intervention in this debate that he looked upon the Conservative party as one which does not care, a party without compassion. I remember when the Die-fenbaker government was elected in 1957, and the erosion of the previous Liberal government which had started with the pipeline debate of 1956. I look back on that period and 1 think that the coup de grace to that government was a measure it introduced just prior to the election to provide for a $6 increase in the old age pension. At that time the old age pension was $40 per month. 1 believe, certainly in the part of the country from where 1 come, that that miserly, uncompassionate act did more to lose votes and lose seats for the Liberal party than anything else; yes, even the pipeline debate. It is not without significance, Mr. Speaker, that the very first act of the Diefenbaker government was to increase the basic old age pension, not from $40 to $46, but from $40 to $53.
I remember in 1979 when the Clark government was returned to this House, albeit in a minority position, that one of the first acts of that government was to extend the payment of the spouse's allowance. Indeed, 1 believe that was the first bill that we put through this House. 1 am reminded by my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) of that, because she campaigned so vigorously in this House on behalf of widows and surviving spouses who had been treated so unjustly by the law that deprived them of the allowance six months after the death of their partner. We extended that allowance.
I do not think we have a monopoly on being compassionate; I think all hon. members of this House have a genuine feeling for the disadvantaged in this country, particularly those in their constituencies. It is difficult for the government backbenchers in a debate like this, because they cannot give voice or expression to that concern. 1 understand the reasons for that and 1 do not make any judgment upon it; all I say to them is that it is going to be difficult for them as they go back to their constituencies to face their constituents.
Let us recall the combination of events that brought about this debate, events which are alarming in their significance and potential consequences on the three groups that we should concern ourselves with in this country-the working poor, the unemployed and the old age pensioners, people on fixed incomes. 1 am reminded of a question that I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) just a week or so ago which was prompted by a statement which the Prime Minister made during his press conference two weeks ago. At that press conference the Prime Minister was asked to comment on the impact of inflation on low-income earners and the old age pensioners of this country. His reply, one which I think he
lived to regret, was that they should change their priorities. If they wanted to maintain the same level of food on their tables, then they should change their spending in other areas.
I put the case to the House, Mr. Speaker, then, and I do so again today, that if you look at the StatsCan document entitled "Urban Family Expenditure", you will find that one in five families in Canada today spend 82.6 per cent of their earnings on food, shelter and clothing. That includes, of course, people who are unemployed, the low-income earners and people on fixed incomes-the lowest income group in the country. That, of course, compares to the level of 62 per cent which has been established as the poverty line by Statistics Canada. In other words, the poverty line is reached by those who spend 62 per cent of their income on food, shelter and clothing.
We are getting used to hearing the government argue-this was referred to by my colleague from Kingston and the Islands-that we have indexing. The government says it has indexed old age pensions and family allowances, that it has authorized an increase in the guaranteed income supplement. That is true. We do have indexing. But it is also true to ask, is this indexing relative to real increases in the cost of living which relate to the low-income earners, the poor people and the old age pensioners of this country? 1 submit, Mr. Speaker, that when you consider the fact that indexing is based on the consumer price index, then the over-all picture is misleading, because low-income earners have to spend a disproportionate amount of their income on food, shelter and clothing. People in the one in five family group which I have outlined have no other alternative; they have virtually no disposable income.
Food has increased in cost this year by 15.2 per cent. This, of course, includes things like sirloin steak and so on. Even taking that into account, when you consider that the anticipated increase for next year as these interest rates and fuel oil price increases work their way into the system is 20 per cent, then you are looking at a 35 per cent increase in the price of food over a two-year period.
If you examine the situation with regard to fuel oil, you have a situation that becomes even more alarming. The same consumer price index that triggered this debate yesterday shows that fuel oil costs went up by 26.9 per cent. We know what is happening with OPEC. We know the consequences of the government's energy program. We also know from these two facts alone that we can anticipate even more increases in the cost of fuel oil next year.
I would like to relate that cost to what it means to a person who has to make do on a fixed income. I cannot relate it to the working poor because I do not have the figures, but I can certainly relate it to those who have to get by on old age assistance and the guaranteed income supplement. 1 did a check today, just a few hours ago, in my own constituency. 1 checked with a neighbourhood supermarket in a poor neighbourhood in St. John's, and this is what I found out. A quart of milk cost 95 cents. One dozen medium-sized eggs cost $1.49. A loaf of bread cost 85 cents. A pound of margarine cost 95 cents. A pound of round steak-that is the sort you
December 19, 1980

have to stew in order to eat it because it is generally tough- cost $3.49. A gallon of fuel oil in the city of St. John's today costs 96 cents. That is reality.
During the last three months when old age pensions, OAS, the guaranteed income supplement and the family allowances were last indexed, there has been a sharp increase in costs over that three-month period. You can gather from that how irrelevant indexing actually is. For example, let us examine what we mean by indexing in real dollars and cents terms, in terms which relate to the price of a dozen eggs, or a pound of round steak, a pound of margarine, a loaf of bread or a gallon of home heating oil. Coincidentally, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) issued a press release today announcing the amount of indexing to take effect in January. As of January, the basic old age assistance cheque will increase from $196.83 to $202.14, an increase of $5.31 over three months. What, Mr. Speaker, can you buy for $5.31? What difference does that amount make? It will not even buy a pound of sirloin steak or a ticket to a movie in St. John's.
Let us take the guaranteed income supplement. As of January it will go from $197.60 to $202.94, a grand increase of $5.34. That is the sheet anchor upon which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) bases his compassionate feelings and his compassion for the poor of this country. What compassion? In January, the guaranteed income supplement for a married couple will increase from $152.36 to $156.47, for a total increase of $4.1 1. A couple will receive an increase in the guaranteed income supplement for the three months' indexing of $4.11.
Mr. Speaker, come back to that 95-cent quart of milk, that $1.49 dozen of eggs, that 85-cent loaf of bread, that 95-cent pound of margarine, that $3.49 per pound for round steak or the 96 cents for a gallon of fuel oil and you get the story. It has been said that Christmas is cruel to the lonely, that it is a difficult time for people who are alone. I would like to project that thinking just one step further and say that Christmas is a cruel time for the low-income earner of this country. Christmas is a cruel time for the working poor and a cruel time for the old age pensioner who is trying to get by on his pension and guaranteed income supplement. It is cruel because he sees around him all the material things of this seemingly affluent society. He sees them in the Christmas trappings of the marketplace at this time of the year. He sees them on his television set portrayed in glittering terms with slick advertising and selling techniques. Imagine the aggravation that person must feel as he sees the succulent butterball turkey presented on television knowing he must depend on the gift of a utility turkey from some charitable organization. Imagine also what such a person must feel when he sees the opulence of a typical middle-income family at Christmastime, then looks around at his family and realizes he cannot provide them with these things. That, to me, is a more cruel situation for him than if he were alone.
Economic Conditions
That is what this debate is all about, Mr. Speaker. If we can reach the government opposite and signal to it a message that this debate reflects the concern of the country over what is happening to the economy, then perhaps it might consider bringing in a shelter allowance and some relief for those who have to buy fuel oils to heat their homes. If not, then the situation will only get worse.
I have referred to only one group of the three. I have referred only to the fixed income, old age pensioner. I have not touched on the working poor except in terms of their inability to be able to meet the demands of this consumer-oriented society in so far as their children are concerned. I have not touched on the unemployed, the third group. There are one million people unemployed in this country today. In official terms we can say 800,000, but in real terms it is over one million if one takes into account the hidden force of the unemployed who have stopped looking for jobs out of sheer frustration.
The Minister of Finance, raised in the tradition of Cape Breton and educated in the tradition of Monseigneur Coady, has said, "Well, we have indexed unemployment insurance". I would ask him to consider getting by on an unemployment insurance payment of $ 130, $ 140 or $ 150 a week. That is what it averages in Cape Breton or Newfoundland. Could he get by and feed a family on that with inflated prices for food and the anticipation that he will have to pay more for vegetables because of the interest rate and the steep increase in the cost of imported food?
If one thinks about the increases in the cost of fuel oil, one gets some idea of the frustration of the person who is unemployed through no fault of his own. One realizes how realistic it is to consider the social consequences of unemployment which often lead to suicide. I must feed eight people and I know what it is to go to the supermarket every week and fill up that basket. I see the change week after week. I come from a background where I was one of 15 children, so I have some idea of the struggles and the problems which low-income families face.
What 1 cannot conceive even with that experience is what unemployed persons must have to go through. Generally speaking, they are unskilled and they usually have large families. How in the name of God they manage to feed their families is beyond me. I sometimes believe we are isolated from reality in this place. The only chance to get to see the real world is when we go to our constituencies. I am convinced the government has isolated itself from reality.
I know how easy it is. From my brief experience as a cabinet minister I know, as do my colleagues, how quickly one becomes isolated from the real world, the world of the unemployed and the person who is trying to get by on old age assistance and the guaranteed income supplement, the world of the widow referred to by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and those who are trying to get by on a maximum income of $350 a month because they are unemployable and that is all the state will provide.

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
That is the real world and the world we are trying to bring into this place by means of this debate. If we achieve that, then this whole exercise will have been worth while. A nation's culture and civilization is measured by its compassion for its disadvantaged people. We like to pride ourselves on having a good system of social security. We have a good basic system, but we tend to look upon it as the be-all and the end-all in itself.
Therein we make a great mistake and therein we do a great disservice to our fellow men and women who must get by on unemployment insurance, on fixed incomes or on the minimum
wage.
A man called me the other day from my constituency. He is a supervisor with a security firm, and he has five children in his household. He is being paid $3.40 an hour and he has to work a 44-hour week. He has to buy his own uniform. This is not an isolated case. How in the name of God can that person get by having to pay 96 cents for a gallon of fuel and having to pay the inflated prices for goods which I have just given? It is not that the farmers are gouging the country, because we know that farm incomes have gone down. We know what is happening to farm incomes and what impact that can have on food production in this country. We know of the consequences for further inflation of food prices. If this situation is not corrected, we will become more and more dependent on imported food and, as the economic crisis deepens, we will have to pay more and more.
1 believe we should keep this debate going because I think by doing that we will get the message across to the government and we will dramatically reflect the concern felt in this country. I, for one, have put in many hours on the constitution committee. I consider that a privilege, and I look forward to returning here on January 5. But I find it somewhat difficult to reconcile a three-week recess in the midst of this crisis. I am not unmindful of the fact that that was a factor which influenced the Chair in granting this special debate under Standing Order 26.
We are facing a serious crisis. It is a grave economic crisis, probably the worst this country has faced since the great depression. Somehow it does not seem right we should close down this institution. It seems to me we should come back here and stay so that we can hold the government accountable day by day. In that way perhaps we might be able to reach the government and get the message across. We might just be able to arouse that compassion which I know is in the heart of the Minister of Finance, and perhaps the government may even be moved to do something about this crisis.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate this afternoon, partly because I wish to present some of my own thoughts in this matter and partly because I wish to refute some of the statements which have been made over the last 20
hours, some of which I think contain the height of cynicism. I refer to statements which have come from the Tory opposition. They fit into this particular pattern although I would exclude the statements made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). Over the last eight years I have observed him to be a person who is extremely consistent in his thinking. I know he is one of those who have spoken out for improverished Canadians and those at the bottom of the barrel and in the lower-income brackets. I think what he says is very honest, and I believe we should provide cushions for those people.
1 disagree, however, with his colleague from the same city, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). I think there is a great deal of cynicism there. The hon. member for St. John's West is great with his expletives and his kind of barnyard humour, but I do not think he would know, since he was once minister of finance, that there are no simple answers to what has occurred.
I am particularly annoyed at the efforts of the former minister and at the efforts of the Tory party in general because I feel they were moving on a path worse than the one they are criticizing our government for following. Allow me to explain that. Last fall when the hon. member for St. John's West was minister of finance, we were studying interest rates. He appeared before the finance committee along with the governor of the Bank of Canada. I just want to convey to the House what was happening at that time. We were trying to show the interest rates which really counted were those we called "real" interest rates; that is to say, the rate minus the inflation rate. At that time Canada's real interest rate was about four to five percentage points higher than the real rate in the United States. In other words, the United States government rate was something like 16 per cent and its inflation rate was something like 15 per cent. I cannot give the exact figures which existed at that time, but they were in that area. Our interest rates were 16 per cent or 17 per cent. They were higher than the American rate and our inflation rate was something in the order of 10 per cent. We had a real interest rate about five or six percentage points higher than the American rate at that point.
We asked the governor of the Bank of Canada and the minister about this. They said, "Yes, it is true, real interest rates are lower but we are going to bring in a budget; we are to have higher gasoline and oil taxes and higher prices. Therefore, our inflation rate will go up; it is justified to have a higher rate than the Americans now have." That is what he said in committee. That was the kind of answer we were getting. Basically, the real interest rate was considerably higher than the American rate at that time.
Let us compare that with the present situation. The American real interest rate, the American inflation rate and the Canadian inflation rate are fairly close, with less than a percentage point between them. It is roughly 4 per cent higher than the Canadian prime rate. The real interest rates are roughly 3 per cent apart and our rate is roughly 3 per cent lower than the American rate. Yet members come here and flail us for what we have done. Obviously, interest rates are where they are because the Americans have decided, and I think stupidly, that they can solve inflation by raising the
December 19, 1980

prime rate to 20 per cent, 21 per cent or 25 per cent. It does not make sense. I do not know of any progressive economist in the world today who would say that it makes any sense, but that is the direction they are taking.
Now the minister, and certainly the governor of the Bank of Canada, have in the past followed that kind of economics. 1 am not convinced that we should continue to follow them. The minister is beginning to change that when he talks about the dollar dropping slowly and he is talking about a change in that direction.
What bothers me about this debate is the simplicity of it. All of a sudden it is claimed we could do something simple and the problem would go away. There are no simple answers. There is one thing we can do; we can let the dollar go. We should do that more often, let the dollar drop. That is not as bad as a lot of people say, but certainly there are some problems when we do that. 1 agree with the minister when he says that is the course to follow, but it must be done slowly, not rapidly as some would advocate. But there are no simple answers.
On the other side of the House you will find the same kind of simplicity in the NDP. They think that you can adopt the Keynesian idea of demand economy and that it would just work fine. All we have to do is spend more money, put out more money and that would solve the problem. But there is just no evidence I can find among progressive economists that says it will work.
That has worked in the past but under different circumstances. The reason it will not work today is that the notion of stagflation gives the opposite effect to the one you would normally expect. If you increase demand, you increase inflation; a whole series of things happen and you end up with more people unemployed. That kind of answer is not working. It is not working because we are in a lot of trouble in this country. This is because we have a budget deficit of $12 billion, $13 billion, or $14 billion. If that is not increasing demand, 1 do not know what is.
1 have real difficulties with this question because of the cynicism of members opposite. I do not think there are simple answers. Although I do not say it has to be this way, I would like to see the government move toward a lower dollar for some very strong reasons. My community would probably be most affected by this. Thunder Bay on a per capita basis is, if not the largest, certainly one of the largest exporters in this country. The pulp and paper industry supports between 80 per cent and 90 per cent. We have a large company which manufactures rail cars and they export at least 50 per cent of their product. We are the largest grain exporting city in the world; therefore, exports are very important to us.
I do not believe that a 77, 78 or 79-cent dollar will create a lot of problems. If interest rates are kept at a lower level, that is what should happen. However, that is not what the last minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West, was
Economic Conditions
saying. In the past, he said that rates have to go up because they were going to induce more inflation.
Like the hon. member for St. John's East, I am concerned about the kinds of cushions we have to support those Canadians who need support. A lot of pressure is coming from the Conservative party, the business community and other places, to cut away some of the programs we have brought in over the past ten to 15 years. They would like us to cut family allowances and deindex other programs. There is a lot of pressure on programs such as medicare. Over the years, we have brought these kinds of programs into this country. More and more of them have been indexed. I can foresee family allowances and like programs having their indexation taken away, and this worries me.
Hon. members have talked about the kind of cushion that has been put in. They refer to the mortgage scheme they intended to set up. 1 read their mortgage scheme quite carefully. I spent a lot of time going through it. It was for the upper middle class, not those with low incomes who do not have mortgages.
Hon. members talked about a cushion for the increased price of oil and gasoline. We must not forget that it was the government which was defeated before last Christmas which brought in the 18-cent gasoline tax. That tax was not imposed because the government was defeated on the issue.
It is said we are putting in a cushion for lower-income families. 1 agree there is a cushion, but it is the type of cushion one would receive when walking into a store which is having a big sale. The sign may say "Reduced 50 per cent", but the article is 10 cents higher than the regular price in the store next door. This is the kind of cushion you put in after you have raised the price.
Almost daily 1 read all the literature relating to energy. I am convinced that if the Tories were in power, we would be paying more for our oil and gas because they keep asking for more and more. The Tories keep saying that they had a settlement with Alberta. However, neither the Alberta government nor anyone on the Tory benches has ever said what that settlement was. I do not believe there was a settlement. I defy them to tell me what it was.

I do not blame the Alberta government. They are doing what they should do. However, if we sit down with them, we will get less. We argued this issue all last week. I am convinced that under the present regime, our offer will be a better deal for lower-income Canadians. No one has been able to convince me differently.
I wish to spend the few minutes I have left talking about the oil and gas bill. It is part of this budget and part of the whole
