financial discussion we are now having but I will not spend too much time on it.
1 am particularly disturbed about the NDP opposition to this bill. In this country there is a progressive movement. There are progressives in all political parties in this House. There arc progressives in the Tory party. I am convinced the hon. member for St. John's East is a progressive. There are certainly progressives in the NDP. In fact, in my opinion most of them are progressive. There are a large number of progressives in this party who spent many years working toward a stronger Canada, stronger nationalism and economic nationalism.
I joined the Committee for an Independent Canada as soon as I heard about it, which was very soon after it was formed. The chairman of the local committee for the first national convention, which was held in Thunder Bay, was a very active member of that group. I am still on the board of advisers in a sort of way, but the organization is not as strong as it used to be. For years, I have been concerned about economic nationalism, about who owns Canada and how Canadians can recover lost ground in terms of Canadian ownership.
The result of all the efforts by members on this side, including the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), is that we finally got a package of which we could be proud. We could really do something about Canadian ownership. I am convinced that we will have the support of the Canadian nationals. It is not as much support as I would have liked. It is not as good a deal as the minister would have liked, but it was the best we could get.
When one sits on the opposition side, one thinks that the governing party has just one single idea, that it is in the head of the Prime Minister and that is it. However, that is not what this is all about. The party in power, as the Tories would have probably found out had they been in power longer, is a party with a lot of ideas coming into it. There are people who are right-wing, people who are left-wing, people who are ambivalent and so on.
These people come together and apply pressures. The things they hear from their constituents and from various regions of the country are what make up the government in this country. Many people have views about Canadian nationalism. They want to see the oil industry Canadian controlled. They want to see this 50 per cent thing. They come together and agree to put on some real pressure. That is what happens inside a government. Individually and collectively we keep this up, and the result, of course, is a bill which says that we are going to move toward 50 per cent ownership and that we are going to move fairly rapidly. We will not move as rapidly as the NDP would like, but then we could not afford to move that rapidly, and the country is not with us to that extent.
However, what I am saying is that the pressure was there. The minister, who was the leader of this movement, also wanted this desperately, and so we have a Canadian bill which is good for Canada. I used to sit in the Standing Committe on
National Resources and Public Works with Tommy Douglas and people like that. I worked side by side with him when we were considering the Petro-Canada bill. We used to work together on this kind of thing.
At this point we have a chance to make a breakthrough, but it is difficult because the oil industry in this country is not happy. Indeed, many people in this country are not happy about that bill. The official opposition is to the right of that bill. Its members say we are going too far, and at this point our friends who are supposed to be the Canadian nationalists desert us because they do not think the bill is good enough. This has bothered me. I cannot say how much I have been perturbed by that. The NDP should take the attitude which I am sure they would have taken under the leadership of Mr. Douglas. If they do not like certain aspects of the bill, and if they think it should go further, then they should say they will support it in principle, allow it to go to committee and fight like hell there to get some decent amendments.
I really wonder about this debate. I wonder whether we are just grandstanding. It seems to me that there are no simple answers to the problems we are facing. The problems we have are not the result of somebody who is vicious or stupid. They are problems the whole world is facing, and rather than sit here and condemn this and yell about that, we should sit down and talk about the kinds of solutions which should be sought. They will not be simple because the problem is not simple.
I hope I have concluded on a reasonably positive note. I hope that somewhere along the line in the new year the cynicism of this kind of debate and particularly the cynicism 1 see in question period will disappear.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues.
We have heard very many speeches over the last night and day. I think they were important speeches. 1 do not quite agree, with all due respect, with my colleagues across the floor. I think there have been important speeches in this emergency debate on the drastic state of our economy.
Speeches have been made about the intolerable interest rates, and speeches have been made deploring the fall of the government last December. There have been speeches about the high cost of fuel and food, and I share the concern which was expressed by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
There have also been references to the constitution, to energy policy and to the high cost of interest rates for small businesses.
December 19, 1980

The Liberals extolled Liberal economic policies, and the rest of us condemned non-Liberal non-policies. Last night we even heard speeches about Russia and about Christmas shopping. However, 1 say again that 1 feel that although this has been tiring, it has been a very worth-while exercise. It has certainly been a record-setting debate in the Canadian House of Commons.
We have reached a record flow of words. 1 think that is because we really do care about what is happening to ordinary people and to the people for whom the hon. member for St. John's East has just so eloquently spoken. I think we care very much, because we are concerned not just about the very poor but also the sons and daughters and people in almost every economic sphere who are affected by the very drastic situation in Canada today.
1 am not going to waste time criticizing. Well, I suppose 1 will be doing a little bit of criticizing. That is my job, but I hope I will not be chastising my political opponents in too negative a way. I think we are really all equally concerned, and we know that it is very difficult to find solutions.
At the request of my colleagues 1 would like to speak specifically and concentrate specifically on the very serious housing situation in Canada. There is a serious housing situation for both tenants and home owners as a direct result of the very high interest rates and the lack of planning by the government and due also to the increasing speculation we see in very crowded parts of our country. We say-and I think we believe very strongly-that owning a home has always been a Canadian dream. 1 think those of us who have homes which we got into some years ago are very fortunate. This is certainly still the dream of many people. It is a dream which will not be fulfilled, of course, for many Canadians. However, it is certainly one of the best hedges against inflation for those who do own homes or have paid off a good part of their homes. It is also very much easier for people who are unemployed and laid off or perhaps on unemployment insurance if they have a home which is paid for or almost paid for. Indeed, it is the one asset which many, many people have. I refer to people on average and low incomes. It is an asset which is there to provide security in retirement and old age.
Home ownership is not just keeping up with the Jones's. It is really a basic part of our economic security. This was particularly brought home to me last spring on a housing tour in northern Newfoundland. I visited the northern peninsula as a guest of the national anti-poverty group. My colleagues from that area of Newfoundland would agree that it is one of the poorest areas in Canada. There is a very high rate of unemployment there. Many fishermen work just the minimum number of the weeks in the year to qualify for unemployment insurance. Many others are on welfare year-round, yet I was impressed that in these small fishing villages in remote areas, because the people own their homes-and some of them we might call shacks or small cottages-they really were in a much better situation than many other poor people across Canada. They had been able to get their land at cheap rates. They are still able to get it fairly cheaply and, of course, they
Economic Conditions
put their own labour, often in a co-operative way, into the building of their homes. I was impressed by federal government programs. The RRAP and the home repair programs were particularly suited to this area because the incomes are low and the people could take full advantage of them.
In Nova Scotia as well as in New Brunswick I was impressed with the very high percentage of home ownership, which is a tradition there. Of course, we know that in that part of Canada, unlike the part I come from on the west coast, the population is somewhat stable and perhaps even decreasing in some communities, whereas our population is increasing with a great inflow of people by the thousands each month. It is great that people own their homes, but it is also great that they have built them themselves. Some of them had very innovative kinds of arrangements. In former years they could have shell houses and finish them off themselves. I was particularly interested in building co-operatives which no longer are possible because of interest rates and insecure mortgage programs. Lormerly, in these building co-operatives, labour was shared. The co-ops were able to buy supplies collectively and share expertise as well to keep down the cost of housing.
These are things which are not just a dream. They are surely things which by some really innovative program could be brought about. There is a human value involved, and this is a very practical approach to housing which we should make sure we get into again.
The big change, of course, in the maritimes, as in every other part of Canada, is the fact that in the larger cities now it is almost impossible for young people to purchase a home of their own. I should like to mention also a trend which I noticed in the Atlantic region and which worries me because I think it is prevalent in older cities as well, and that is the trend to rehabilitate the downtown areas of cities using heritage funds. Whitewashing, as it is called, or blockbusting, is a kind of move intended to improve the appearance of the downtown core but it often ends up by removing houses, particularly family houses, and low-cost rental homes. This creates high-priced housing for professional people and for people who can be called swingers. It means that the poor people who have traditionally lived in the centre of our cities are pushed to the suburbs and often to areas without transit and with a high cost of energy. This is happening, I think, in Saint John where there is a great increase in population.

speechtext:
1 think that in the Christmas spirit, members of Parliament should be concerned about all Canadians, not only the region in which they live. I could very well speak for several hours about the terrible conditions in British Columbia.
Across the country there is a zero vacancy rate in rental housing in most urban centres. I raised this in the House as a question the other day. This occurs in St. John's, Toronto, Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Regina, Calgary, Victoria and yes, in Vancouver. Most of these are centres of economic growth, as we know, with a large influx of newcomers due to migration across Canada and very heavy immigration as well, so that the housing stock is seriously depleted and there is considerable overcrowding.
We also know that most cities, particularly cities of large growth and fast growing cities, suffer from lack of long-range planning. 1 would like to mention particularly the lack of long-range planning by the federal government in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities to provide adequate shelter for people who are needed and who are looking for jobs and looking for a better future, and who move to these parts of Canada. This comes at a time when we have escalating interest rates and 1 will get back to the subject in a minute. It is also of considerable concern that the community service grants and the neighbourhood improvement programs which were to help developing communities have been cut off, that federal assistance for land banking programs, which is very important in my view, is no longer available, and also that there are very scarce federal funds now going into public housing which is still needed as the only form of housing that can meet the needs of poor communities. We know, of course, that the high and unstable interest rates are forcing up the price of housing at a drastic and deplorable rate.
In addition, in my city of Vancouver-if the hon. gentleman would like me to talk about that-there is excessive speculation. It is not unusual for a house to be purchased in the morning and sold with a mark-up of about $15,000 later in the same day. We had a concern, as expressed by our new mayor in Vancouver, about considerable speculation on the part of foreign investors which we feel should be curtailed by some specific programs. Certainly the federal government should intervene in such areas as Vancouver and other cities to develop affordable housing. Of course, we need provincial involvement, but it cannot be done without a much greater input from the federal government. That is absolutely essential. However, unfortunately, very little help is available.
1 would like to speak, first of all, about home ownership. High interest rates and soaring land costs are devastating for would-be home owners. The dream of home ownership which I mentioned earlier, is dead, particularly for Canadians under the age of 35. Members of this House who have children in that age group are finding, I am sure, that it is literally impossible for them to own a home today.
We calculated that at the current mortgage interest rates, which are now 16 per cent to 20 per cent for a mortgage on a new home, it will cost close to $1,000 per month for the
mortgage payments and for fuel and taxes, on which the prices are also going up. This means that a person wishing to purchase a home must earn a net income of about $40,000. Even members of Parliament are not quite in that income bracket so far as take home pay is concerned. This is a really deplorable situation. The only way in which home ownership is made possible, at least in my area, is for two wage earners, and now three wage earners, to purchase a house collectively. Adult children live at home with their parents or help out their elderly parents, and houses are being converted into duplexes for extended families and group living. There is pretty serious overcrowding. Our whole lifestyle is changing because of the terribly high cost of housing. Those of us who own homes and have almost paid them off are very fortunate, because our children will not have this chance.
The next area I wanted to mention was AHOP home ownership. We have heard a lot about this in the House as well.
Unfortunately, this is the only response the Liberal government has made to try to develop lower-cost mortgages for people on lower incomes. By lower incomes 1 do not mean very low incomes, ! mean average income people and young people coming out of university who want to own a home. I have spoken of this several times in the House and 1 am sure hon. members know how fallacious AHOP was and how it has bombed. Purchasers who were offered low down payments and low interest rates for the first five years found that they could not afford to refinance after this period. Many low-income people and struggling young families lost their homes as a result. Some found it cheaper to walk away from these AHOP houses and leave them to the creditors. As a result, CMHC has acquired a good deal of real estate and, of course, it has a good deal of money invested in these homes when the mortgages were foreclosed. We find that the financial situation of CMHC is worse than ever. It has cash flow problems and money invested in these houses which should really be invested in non-profit housing for people with the greatest need.
I am concerned also about complaints I have received, and I imagine other hon. members have also had them, that selling prices of some of these AHOP houses acquired by CMHC have been below market value. We like lower-cost housing but I do not think it is quite fair to price these houses at a considerably lower cost and sell them in a non-competitive bidding situation.
The minister said in the House several times that the government would act to help AHOP home owners, those in the greatest need. However, we have a great deal of difficulty finding out just what he has done. It is somewhat apparent that he has done very little. We finally learned yesterday that short-term assistance was offered to only 420 home owners, and I think there are something like 800,000 home owners with mortgages coming up for renewal. With the present cost of living and high interest rates, it is hard to agree that these are the only people who are suffering as hardship cases.
December 19, 1980

The investment of CMHC in this kind of subsidy for people to keep their homes is about $1,200 per house. So, it is a relatively small expenditure on the part of the federal government. Perhaps the intentions of the minister were good, but certainly his idea of hardship is far from being close to reality. Of course, we know that it is not just AHOP home owners who are facing renewals and foreclosures. Other members have spoken about this matter in our long debate. However, because of the government's fluctuating interest rate policy, people are now having to gamble on their homes. We are finding that people are being advised to take out only six-month or perhaps one-year mortgages, hoping that the rates will change and that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will be good to them in the new year. We know that he has not been good to them and has no intention of being good to them. In fact, the rates have risen considerably over the 12-month period on which these people have been gambling.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we enter the twenty-second hour of this debate it is worth reminding ourselves of what brought this debate on and the target of the debate. The target is pretty sparse on the other side, but there has been an attempt by opposition members to get through to the government some of the critical features of our present economic plight.
We must remember the background. It was brought on in the beginning because we had been watching the value of the
Economic Conditions
Canadian dollar drop from 84 cents to 83 cents, and gradually down until it reached a 47-year low of 82.56 cents on Wednesday. The next matter in sequence which caused concern was the inflation rate. It was announced that the inflation rate had increased on a yearly basis by 1.2 per cent from the previous month. The third element was the recorded high interest rate for borrowing from the central bank. It was announced around noontime yesterday to be 18.25 per cent, following the tracking of the rate in the United States.
These three elements-the dropping Canadian dollar, the high inflation rate, and the escalation in the interest rate- caused the two parties in the opposition to table motions requiring an emergency debate on the economic situation in which Canada finds itself. As 1 say, we are now starting the twenty-second hour of that debate.
I should like to refer to page 5446 of Hansard when the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was questioning the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the economic recession. The Prime Minister referred to people who are confronted with the problems to which these particular indicators point and which have created serious economic recession and inflation. In answer to the question, the Prime Minister said:
-it is a common sense matter when you have a set budget to spend more or less of it on the aspects which are more necessary to your daily life-
As far as I can make out, the Prime Minister never had a set budget. This is the advice the Prime Minister offered to those persons on fixed incomes.
What figures were released yesterday which prompted this remark? Leaving aside the effect of the declining dollar and high interest rates, what actually occurred with respect to the cost of living? The change between November, 1979, and October, 1980, was an over-all increase of 11.2 per cent on all items. I should like to single out some of the elements of that basket. On food alone, the increase over that same period was 13.7 per cent, and on housing it was 9 per cent. During the course of my remarks I will break down those two items even further. Bearing in mind what that represents and the index as of November, 1980, it now stands at $220. It has risen from a base in 1971 of $100. In other words, it is now 2.2 times the cost of the basket which could have been bought for $100 in 1971; now it would cost $220. That is a rough way in which to describe it.
On food the index is $273.90 on the base index of $100 in 1971 and housing is $208. So, all costs have at least more than doubled. Those are very important elements to bear in mind when one is on a fixed income, particularly when asked to shuffle one's priorities so as to buy more food or a little more fuel oil, or a little less dog meat and a little more bread. Perhaps it would be a little less bread and a little more dog meat; I am not quite sure.

Economic Conditions

speechtext:
Dog meat may be too
expensive, as my colleague reminds me.
In this index, because of the weightings of the various components that I have mentioned, the energy aspect of housing deserves special treatment. On average, the energy element that goes into the consumer price index has increased over the last year by 20 percentage points. For example, fuel oil, 26.7; gas for heating and cooking, 20.7; electricity, 9.6. I remind the House that food has increased from overa year ago 13.7 per cent.
In face of those essential components-I am not talking about clothing or housing, but the very bare essentials such as food and warmth-the Prime Minister has the gall to say to this House as advice to people on fixed incomes that it is a common sense matter, when you have a set budget, to spend more or less of it on the aspects which are more necessary to your daily life. What elements are there which are more necessary than food and warmth, assuming that you start the day with some clothing itself?
My colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) referred to the state of a widow on pension. She used the figure of $350 a month. In the CPI the weighting for heat and energy is 2 per cent. This means that 2 per cent of $350 allows that pensioner $7 per month for heating. On the food side, 21 per cent of $350, which is roughly one-fifth, is $70 per month. How can the Prime Minister expect anyone to shift these figures from that which is less important to that which is more important? Hon. members in this House have been talking about the lack of compassion of some members of this party, but 1 suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if there is anyone who lacks compassion, it is the person who uses those terms to those on fixed incomes.
I would like to examine a little more closely the consumer price index to see what room there might be for manoeuvre. The consumer price index is built up of a basket of goods which in total involves elements such as food, which is 21.5 per cent, housing, which is 34 per cent, clothing, 10 per cent, transportation, 15.8 per cent, health and personal care, 3.96 per cent, recreation, reading and education, 8 per cent, tobacco and alcohol, 6.24 per cent. Unless I have missed one or other of these elements, those figures total 100 per cent. Each of the elements is broken down even more. When the index is being devised, 1 see that the weighting for beef alone is 2.5 per cent, or about one-fortieth of the whole basket. Other meat is .85 per cent, poultry is .80 per cent, and fish is .40 per cent.
I compare this with some of the other elements. For example, the basket is composed of fish at .4 per cent, and then I see the item of pet care, .4 per cent. I wonder if that is a realistic way to devise an index for those on fixed incomes. I am sure that those who are on Fixed incomes and living alone would be very happy to have a pet to keep them company, but whether they spend the same proportion of their income, small as it is, on pet food as they do on coffee and tea, 1 think is questionable. Health and personal care is almost 4 per cent. I am sure that those who are on fixed income are normally elderly and will be paying more than that, even if they are on a health plan.
One of the more charitable and compassionate suggestions that I think the Prime Minister might have made is that he was prepared to ensure that there would be a different sort of index applicable to those on fixed incomes, not this general index which happens to be built up in a way that is, perhaps, not well understood. It is a basket of goods and services purchased by families and unattached individuals, a spending unit, living in private households in urban centres with populations of 30,000 or over. Not all people on fixed incomes live in those circumstances. They do not all live in urban centres where the population is 30,000 or over. Therefore, I find this CPI completely unrealistic.
1 have argued this case before but I have found that in this place it is necessary to go back and repeat some of the speeches which were made earlier; and I urgently request the government to look into the matter of having a special consumer price index for those on fixed incomes, so that when their pension is indexed it will be indexed more realistically and in line with the actual purchases which they make. Therefore, I say that the CPI as it now stands is hardly a valid basis on which to base indexation for those on fixed incomes.
I should like to break it down further, but in this particular debate I think there is room to broaden the ambit somewhat and give it a philosophical connotation, if you like. I believe there has been altogether too much attention given by this government to building up expectations which cannot be fulfilled. I was absolutely staggered the other day. We were on an international delegation and one of my colleagues who was with me, not of my party, said, "I think it is so evident that the government will look after me for the rest of my life that 1 should be spending everything I earn. There is no reason in the world for me to save it." That sort of attitude is what has driven the government. Government ministers produced the attitude for one thing. They have not encouraged or given this person any incentive whatever to invest in his own country, and it is what is moving the government at the present time to do this person's investing for him and nationalizing enterprise in this country.
One particular instance comes to mind, and it is the very recent takeover by Petro-Canada of Merit Oil. There were a number of outlets and it was one of the original economy cut rate gas purveyors in British Columbia in the lower mainland. There were about 40 outlets run entirely by Canadians, supplied from Canadian sources. PetroCan, in the interest of Canadianization, bought it out. There will not be any more cut rate fuel available from that firm. That is not Canadianization. It was Canadian before it was taken over. That is nationalization. Let the government be honest at least, if that is what it is intending to do.
December 19, 1980

The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) mentioned some suggestions. I can produce several suggestions on how we can improve pride in our country. There should be an incentive for individual investment. Why should individuals who were being serviced by the Merit outlets, for example, not help to keep that company afloat? Now it is being throttled by Petro-Canada which joined the other suppliers of gasoline they were selling. Gradually it took over.
The government could also reopen negotiations with the producing provinces to keep enterprise in this country instead of driving it out, and driving the dollar down. One of the great problems of driving the dollar down is that all the imports, even the orange juice which we have in the morning, will cost us more as the dollar goes down. The ripple effect of keeping industry here in Canada will obviously be felt here in Ontario.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a long 22 hours or so, and 1 would like to commend those members on both sides of the House, especially those on this side, who, I think, have spoken with far greater frequency. I want to commend them for the effort which they have put into this debate which has important implications for Canada. Our country is faced with economic calamity, indeed with a dangerous crisis.
We are discussing here the plight of home owners and businessmen-relatively affluent groups in our society-but especially the plight of the poor, the underprivileged and the impoverished in our society. We are addressing the impact of inflation and high interest rates on farmers and fishermen, auto workers, steel workers, school teachers and even Speakers of the House of Commons. The rise in the interest rate of recent days, coupled with a collapsing dollar, both speak in condemnation of the policies of the Liberal government over these past years.
I would like to read from a letter which I received from a constituent of mine. It is typical of the sentiments expressed by thousands of constituents of all members of Parliament. It reflects sentiments which members opposite will have to face up to and contend with during the Christmas holiday period. It reads in part:
Dear Mr. Siddon:
I work in an industrial plant in Vancouver as a so-called skilled tradesman. I am telling you. Sir, that the average man employed on that shop floor docs not give a (blankety-blank) about repatriating the constitution. Furthermore, few Canadians understand the meaning or the implications of such an undertaking. Most of my friends out west here are far more concerned with unemployment, inflation, increase in crime in metropolitan areas, decline of law and order, etc., and not necessarily in that order.
In responding to a question which I asked my constituents about the government's tendency to accumulate massive deficits, this gentleman writes:
The average working stiff, the so-called middle-and upper-middle class Canadian pays the brunt of personal income tax in this country. As far as myself and friends are concerned, we need every break we can get from the irresponsible fiscal planners in Ottawa.
Economic Conditions
1 believe that those last few words are reflective of the plight which faces our nation. 1 would like to illustrate by drawing reference to another specific situation. Before doing that, however, I should say that I was most intrigued to pick up the Householder mailed out by the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier) to his constituents. In it he has chosen to expound on all the great benefits that have accrued to his riding and his people as a consequence of the return of the Liberal government. There is a long list of million dollar programs and employment opportunities which have been created in his riding. In particular, I notice that he makes a big issue of a $4.8 million grant to a Mont Tremblant tourist centre, from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, as well as $137 million for job creation, and aid to municipalities. He claims that over 2,000 municipalities will receive $25 million in federal aid. There was also a $9.4 million grant to an aircraft company in his riding.
1 cannot offer those kinds of Christmas presents to the people in my riding. I am afraid that it is time there was an accounting for this sort of thing. I must go to the people in my riding and explain why it is that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) has terminated the Community Services Development Program. And here we have this member for Longueuil bragging about the millions being dropped in his riding. The government wonders why the people in my part of the country and other more distant parts of the country feel alienated.
I have a great Christmas present to explain to the people in my riding. Yesterday the tenants of the Kiwanis Senior Citizens Housing project in Richmond, British Columbia, received a bill. This bill is being received by people all across British Columbia, including the residents in all the non-profit housing projects. The bill is from British Columbia Hydro. It is a bill for natural gas and it includes a supplementary surcharge, arising out of the federal budget. These are people who are living in social housing projects and they are only there because their income is less than $5,000 a year.

speechtext:
It has nothing to do with the Premier of British Columbia, but it has a lot to do with the government opposite. The supplementary surcharge printed on this bill will be received by every home owner in British Columbia who heats his or her home with natural gas. The surcharge is clearly stated to be a direct consequence of the federal government's natural gas tax. This supplementary surcharge, which arrived just the day before yesterday, virtually on Christmas eve, will impact on single people, old people, sick people buying drugs and medicine and having to contend with the cost of food, clothing and shelter. These poor souls are getting dinged an extra $3 a month because of the natural gas tax. That is how direct the impact has been. It is but one small aspect of the federal budget. The compounding effect of all the various taxes imposed upon the oil industry of this country, the energy industries, is destroying the well-being and the standard of living of all Canadians.

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
I do not know how I will explain this to my constituents. Prior to the budget announcement, some 32,000 residents of British Columbia had expressed their objection to an export tax on natural gas. So the government came back, in all its sanctimony, and sent the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) into this House where he announced that the government had decided to abandon an export tax on natural gas. Instead ministers had decided to tax all natural gas, he told us. At the same time, of course, the government decided to restrict the export price of natural gas and announced that it would not provide for any increase in that. So where will the money come from to pay the extra tax on natural gas? Well, half of it will come from the pockets of the consumers, the private individual home owners and the industrial consumers of British Columbia. This will amount to S50 million for the present fiscal year, and $130 million for 1983. An additional $180 million will be lost to the B.C. economy in relation to export sales.
That money is coming out of the pockets of the consumer, Mr. Speaker. And that is just as a consequence of that one small measure-a tax on natural gas. It amounts to over $200 million a year out of the B.C. economy, to be taken from the residents of British Columbia, by the end of 1983. And if 1 were to add up all the composite effects which the federal energy taxes impose on British Columbia, it would exceed a billion dollars. A billion dollars lost to British Columbia by the end of 1983! Now where does that money come from? It comes finally and ultimately from the incomes earned by British Columbians. And British Columbia is not a resource-wealthy province in the sense of oil and gas when compared with some other provinces.
We are dealing here today with the question of high interest rates. I ask the members of this House why they think it is that the interest rate is 20 per cent in the United States today. The fact of the matter is that the Americans are not self-sufficient in oil; they do not have nearly enough oil to meet their own requirements. They are short to the tune of some 50 per cent plus. So they are exploring all over the continental United States for oil and gas. They are trying to develop hydrocarbon resources from shales, and they are looking into alternative energy technologies. All of that takes capital. To attract capital and to get the United States off its dependence on foreign oil they are having to pay interest rates of the order of 20 per cent and higher.
If you lived in a country, Mr. Speaker, where the inflation rate was running at 10 per cent or 12 per cent, such as Canada, and you had to compete with the demand for capital from a large neighbour to the south where the interest rate is 20 per cent, what interest rate would you need? That is the problem. In order to earn a fair rate of return on investment in Canada, the interest rate has to be where it is. That is what we are told by the economists. Well, why have we gotten into that situation? Why are we so tightly linked to the Americans, and why do we not find ways to make it attractive for Canadians to keep their capital at home, and for others to invest in this
country, in order that we may produce jobs here? Why must we go instead with our hands out, to the Americans and elsewhere to borrow money, as a means of continuing to finance our accustomed lifestyle? That is merely trading on the future equity of our natural resources, and selling out the future of our children.
It is not fair to blame the Americans. The blame starts with a country and a government which has allowed runaway inflation. Inflation eats away at the return which can be earned on investment. Profits have also been eaten away by unconscionable tax levels imposed, not only on our industries, but on individuals in this country.
I heard the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) say last night that high interest rates are caused by inflation. I agree with that to a degree, but the other side of his argument was that high interest rates do not contribute to inflation. To that I say, some economist! At this particular point in our history, high interest rates are having a very profound effect upon inflation in our country. There is a synergetic effect; there is a linkage between interest rates and inflation, so that one reinforces the other, and it in turn reinforces the first. This puts the economy into an unstable cycle, as it is at the present time. In that unstable cycle you have a continual amplification of both interest rates and inflation, unless you take drastic action to bring that situation under control. The budget of the government takes no such drastic action, except to make Canada much more isolationist.
Mr. Speaker, 1 expect the government will soon start wage and price controls; perhaps foreign exchange controls. These are not my recommendations but I think these perhaps are the concepts that the government is going to be forced to consider-more isolationism, more protectionism, more socialism, more government intervention and, ultimately, further down the road, another form of government which many of us in the House dread.
We have heard some talk about the concept of the Laffer curve, which is a plot relating the productivity of our economy to the percentage of the gross national product which is taken away by governments in the form of taxation. Economists now know that when we have a level of taxation which exceeds a certain optimal level, the productivity of a country will begin to decline. When you are on the high side of that Laffer curve with tax levels exceeding the optimum value and governments are grabbing and groping for more and more wealth, which ultimately has to be earned by the people who work, you then get into an unstable situation where companies and individuals have less and less room to manoeuvre.
Consider a company in a fairly healthy, buoyant, free enterprise economy, which has a fairly comfortable profit margin. Well, if the interest rate were to rise suddenly because of some anomaly, that company would have enough cushion to absorb such an increase for a period of time, and weather the rise out. It would have some cushion in its profit margin to absorb higher interest rates, so it would not have to pass that increase directly on to the consumer. But if the profit margin has been reduced to zero, or near zero, because of the imposition of excessive taxation upon the operation of that venture,
December 19, 1980

then what is going to happen if interest rates go up? What is going to happen is that prices will have to rise, and that is precisely what is happening in this country today. There is no longer any flexibility in the private sector economy, because the government has taken away all the room to manoeuvre.
It all starts with oil, Mr. Speaker. We have a budget now that started out, on October 28, with a 9 per cent excise tax on gasoline, and an export tax on oil. Then the government added to that a natural gas tax, an 8 per cent producer tax, and income tax on net profits, if there are any. But before calculating net profits the industry must pay an import compensation charge, a Canadian ownership charge, and the required provincial taxes both at the producer end and at the consumer end of that chain. If an industry wants to produce oil and gas in the frontier areas, under the provisions of the Canada Lands Act, Bill C-48 presently before the House, then there is also a producer royalty of 10 per cent, with a 40 per cent progressive additional royalty. Mr. Speaker, if you compound all these taxes, there is not enough left to make it worth while to be in the oil and gas business in this country. I submit that this is at the heart of the problem in Canada today.
We could go back and make comparisons between the famous Crosbie budget of a year ago and the present one. If 1 have a few moments left I would like to do that. We recognized a year ago that it was essential to pay for the high cost of imported oil in order to equalize the price of gasoline and oil to all Canadians. So the Crosbie budget provided that it be paid for by a surcharge on gasoline, which is a discretionary commodity. We burn too much and waste too much of it anyway. And that 18 cents a gallon excise tax would have raised revenues close to $2 billion each year in order to pay the price of the import oil compensation. Instead of taking that approach, the present government chose to impose a corresponding tax at the wellhead, a tax which affects heating oil, a tax which affects plastics, a tax which affects the costs of producing pulp and paper, steel and every commodity which goes into our basic manufacturing industry. In addition, every time that tax moves one stage through the system it is compounded by surtaxes upon taxes. So rather than taxing a discretionary commodity like gasoline, to pay the price of import compensation, we have a government here which is taxing everything, including the heating oil the retired couple have put into their tank to heat their home. That is the basic discrepancy between the two budgets. The means by which they chose to deal with the high cost of energy is totally incorrect.
There is one other important distinction between the budget of the Conservative government and the budget presented here by the Minister of Finance a few weeks ago. That has to do with housing. The mortgage tax credit which was proposed under the budget of a year ago would have provided a 25 per cent direct deduction from income tax of the cost of mortgage interest on a $50,000 mortgage. That effectively reduces the interest rate by 25 per cent at the end of four years. Starting January I, 1981, that credit on your mortgage interest cost would have been half as much and would have reduced the
Economic Conditions
interest rate by more than 2 per cent. That is 2 per cent relief we are not getting from the government opposite through its budget. It is as simple as that. It was a direct subsidy on the interest paid by home owners.
There was assistance in that budget for the high cost of energy to Canadian families with an income less than $21,000, through an energy tax credit. There was also a small business development bond and investment incentives for investment in Canadian enterprise. There were a number of means of sheltering low income Canadians from the burden of inflation. Instead, we are confronted with a Liberal budget which fuels inflation through the entire economic cycle and which ultimately we will all have to absorb.
Why can't we be masters of our own economy in this country? One reason is that there is no money to be invested in Canada. If the government wants to buy out the petroleum industry, it will be going to New York, West Germany, and elsewhere. Money in Canada is tied up in Canada Savings Bonds, financing a portion of the federal government's $70 billion or $80 billion debt; recycling money through Canada Savings Bonds. It is tied up in term deposits, in secure long-term loans, and government pension plans to the tune of $18 billion. This pension money is non-existent because the government has spent it to Finance its squandering ways.
1 do not know whether hon. members realize it, but in this country we have an equity in the appreciation of housing over the past ten years of more than $300 billion. If the interest rate goes up 1 per cent, what is the additional carrying charge on that $300 billion to Canadian home owners? It is $3 billion. If the interest rate goes up 7 per cent, as it has in the last year or two, the carrying charge is increased by $35 billion.
Where is that amount of money to come from? Ultimately it has to come out of the household budget of Canadians, thereby reducing their discretionary income. It must come out of our gross national product. That product is the heart of our problem today. Our money is tied up as a consequence of government deficit squandering and irresponsible management of the economy of the country.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) called the attention of the House earlier to the number of members on this side who were present, but he forgot to mention how many Progressive Conservatives were here last Wednesday at midnight. Strangely enough, I cannot speak to him since he has now left the House.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make this debate go on indefinitely and my intervention will therefore be brief. The hon. members have been here since eight o'clock last evening and the House has been sitting without interruption since that time. It is now 5.45 p.m., which makes more than 20 hours of sitting. We are now discussing a motion to adjourn the House
80094 - 13

December 19, 1980
Economic Conditions
under the provisions of Standing Order 26 to debate the Canadian economy.
I have had the opportunity to listen to many of the speeches made by the hon. members opposite. They have discussed the economic situation in Canada. Some have talked about inflation, some have talked about the high interest rates, some have talked about unemployment, some have talked about local and regional problems in their constituencies. This is all to their credit. I believe that they were only doing their duty.
It is true that we have problems, Mr. Speaker. Nobody denies this. If it is not the problem of separatism in Quebec, it is the problem of inflation. If it is not the problem of inflation, it is the problem of an oil agreement with Alberta. If it is not the problem of oil, it is the problem of high interest rates. I do not believe that a single member on this side would deny these facts. Unfortunately, however, some have taken it upon themselves to talk about other subjects than inflation, interest rates and unemployment.
Some members have taken it upon themselves to make charges and insinuations about the role of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). This has nothing to do with politics, it is not a conflict of ideas, it is not a difference of opinions. I shall give you an example which occurred this afternoon. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) noted in his speech that our Prime Minister should have more contacts with our friends than with the Soviets. Yet, on page 25 of the issue of December 22 of Maclean's, we can read the following:

The abiding impression left by the Soviet leader was that of an old, tired, sick man, with not long to live. But he did show the occasional small spark. At the ceremonial arrival, members of the diplomatic corps were introduced to him. He shook their hands in silence-until he was presented to Canadian High Commissioner John Hadwen. Brezhnev's eyes lit up. "Trudeau!" he said. "Wheat!" replied the high commissioner.

Why, Mr. Speaker? What was the point this afternoon during a debate on the economy to quote the example of a visit by Mr. Brezhnev to India? As long as members make personal attacks against someone in particular in the House and call other members all sorts of names, they will only make the debates more acrimonious.

I do not think hate has any place in this chamber. Opinions, yes; debate, yes; respect, yes.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, if 1 may, I would like to give an example which concerns the visit of the Right Hon. Prime Minister to Saudi Arabia. Certain jokers on the side of the opposition referred to this trip, but not one of them noted that Saudi Arabia intends to spend $280 billion within the next five years. No one mentioned this fact on the other side. All the companies throughout the world want a share of this pie. This is why the Prime Minister went there, Mr. Speaker. He wanted to
open the door to our Canadian companies so that they may also have a taste of this pie worth $280 billion.
Mr. Speaker, the year 1981 will not be easy. We have not left all our problems behind, they are still before us, but for my part I have confidence in the future of this country; 1 have confidence in the good will of some of the members opposite. I know that some of them have shown their good will, have intellectual integrity and make constructive criticisms. Mr. Speaker, to show some holiday spirit after such an arduous, lengthy and tiring debate, I would like to say that I hope that 1981 will be a year of peace and that all the hon. members, whatever their party, will work in the best interests of the Canadian people. Is this not why we are here?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 must say that, as we approach the twenty-fourth hour of continuous debate, it was with a sense of discouragement and shame that we were forced into this kind of discussion tonight. It is a direct reflection on the leadership and the ability of hon. members opposite to come to grips with some of the problems facing Canadians today. 1 am proud that it was my leader, seconded by the financial critic for the New Democratic Party, who provided us with an opportunity to discuss some of these crucial issues facing Canada in this emergency debate.
1 have listened with a great deal of interest to our colleagues to my right. 1 listened very carefully to many of the positive proposals they have put forward in the last 22 hours. I have been very pleased to be part of a party of representatives who also put forward a vast array of solutions, suggestions and proposals for the government to use to meet this crisis which is upon us in 1980.
I must say that I was distressed at some of the comments 1 heard from across the way, and at some of the performances across the way. Early this evening when the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) wanted to raise with the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) a number of questions about his speech, the hon. member for Kitchener said that he was not interested in entering into a dialogue at all and was more interested in pursuing a game of squash.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   THE ECONOMY EFFECT OF RISING COST OF LIVING AND INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Where are the parliamentary secretaries? Where are the backbenchers? I am proud to say that attendance on this side of the House has been large. That has shown that
December 19, 1980

concern for this country exists on this side of the House. What on earth is going on across the way?
Why was it that we were prompted to take this special action under Standing Order 26? Put very simply, it was because the last nine months and 19 days have seen Canada enter into what could only be called a devastating and pathetic situation.
Let us look at some of the facts. We now have a prime interest rate of 18.25 per cent, and rising on a weekly basis. It is the highest ever in Canadian history. It is the highest rate ever, and we have been listening to the pathetic responses of the Minister of Finance for the last week that he intends to do nothing about it, it is out of his hands and there is nothing that can be done. That is the kind of commitment, initiative, and solution we get from the present government.
The consumer price index in Canada has now increased 11.2 per cent. In the food sector the increase is 13.7 per cent. Bankruptcies in small businesses across Canada today in some provinces are occurring at a 130 percentile rate over the same period last year. In the last year we have seen not tens of thousands of Canadians laid off but 200,000 Canadians laid off, primarily in central Canada. In relation to the United States dollar the value of the Canadian dollar is at its lowest ebb since 1933, since the depression years. We have a deficit now in excess of $14 billion, a current accounts deficit of approximately $6.2 billion.
We have a housing crisis in this country. In numbers like never before, young people are finding it impossible to qualify for mortgages. People are facing difficulty. Even people in this House are facing difficulty when they go to banks to renegotiate mortgages, only to find that their incomes are insufficient. They cannot qualify for the new rates which the government's policies have created. This is to say nothing of rental housing. People who are out now attempting to purchase homes find that there are no homes being constructed to meet the demand across Canada.
The rental housing situation is worse. In my own city of Kamloops, British Columbia, the vacancy rate is virtually zero. In other major metropolitan areas across the country serious rental accommodation shortages are forcing people to live in vans, converted crawl spaces, and converted garages. That is the kind of situation in which we are finding ourselves in Canada. Indeed, it is a housing crisis.
Of course, those who can least afford it are those who are being hit the hardest. I refer to the elderly on fixed incomes and on pensions, veterans on pensions, and the handicapped. I refer to people experiencing regional disparities across the country. Of course, the most dramatic picture of all where this problem focuses very clearly, in terms of the real problem in Canada, is seen when we look at the unemployment level in Canada. In Canada 1,320,000 people are without jobs. That is approximately 8 per cent of the total work force, and here in Canada we are asked to accept, presumably, that 8 per cent unemployment is acceptable, to say that more than one million Canadians being out of work is quite acceptable. That is the
Economic Conditions
kind of response we are hearing from across the way when inquiries are raised in the question period as to what is going to be done. The infamous shrug comes from across the way. Presumably 8 per cent is acceptable.
1 would like to remind hon. members opposite that the unemployed in Canada are not purchasing a great number of Canadian goods. The unemployed do not build and create a sound basis for our Canadian economy. They are unable to play a committed and meaningful role in our various communities and neighbourhoods. They cost Canadians money. They cost all of us in this House money, and I think most of us are getting fed up with having to pay for the unemployed of Canada, because there is no reason to have unemployed in Canada. Other western industrialized countries would never begin to accept an 8 per cent unemployment rate if they had the richness and the opportunities which exist in our country.
One serious side of the employment question which is often overlooked is the social impact of unemployment. What does it really mean when more than one million Canadians are unable to find work, and when more than one million Canadians are unable to provide for their families in a respectable way? One does not have to quote those Canadian and American analysts who have found correlations between rising unemployment and the increased incidence of suicide, homicide, mental illness, family breakdowns, prison sentences and so forth. One can simply examine the contents of a recent analysis with respect to the social impact of job lay-offs prepared by the Metropolitan Toronto Social Planning Council. In this report that council indicates the following:
Social interaction patterns can be very much disrupted by unemployment. The loss of social contact through the work setting is further aggravated by the tendency of unemployed persons to withdraw from friends, relatives and community life . . . Within the family, social interaction patterns can be upset since the loss of a job and income may diminish the unemployed person's status and authority. Shifts in roles within the family, coupled with changes in the unemployed worker's personality, can provoke considerable stress and in extreme cases can lead to family breakdown.
Turned inward, these feelings of bitterness, rage, and powerlessness may result in depression that becomes further exacerbated by the self-doubt and blame that develop when job hunting is not successful. Anxiety over financial difficulties, both now and in the future, also contributes to the depressed mental state that has been found to characterize many laid off workers.
The impact of the economy on family life is further illustrated by the following comments from the National Council on Welfare:
Anything that widens the gap between income and need-the loss of breadwinners wages because of unemployment or illness, escalating rent, sudden rises in fuel and grocery costs, any unexpected and unavoidable expense-can plunge a poor family into crisis.
Specific evidence on personal and family crises due to unemployment is increasingly being catalogued in Canada. In Windsor, Ontario, a city which has experienced major lay-offs in the automotive sector, the mayor's committee on services for the unemployed reported that:
Inability to make credit payments, inability to make unemployment or welfare payments stretch to the end of each month, has brought about uncontrollable

stress and pressures and resulted in increased use of alcohol and tranquillizers and other drugs to ease stress.
The mayor's committee also found that social agencies in Windsor have experienced increases in caseloads ranging from 25 per cent in some months to 377 per cent in other months. In this regard it said:
The human tragedy associated with unemployment is also reflected in the committee's statement that having to go on welfare after other benefits are exhausted is having "a devastating effect on individuals and their families."
One tragic result of prolonged unemployment can be an increase in family violence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly clear that a serious problem is facing us, which is unemployment with the many serious social implications which perhaps we still do not fully understand or appreciate. I have listened with interest as many previous speakers have attempted to define why it is that we find ourselves in this dreadful situation. The most obvious answer is the ineptitude across the way. What is behind this? Why is it that our interest rates, for example, are chasing those in the United States in a rollercoaster effect? When theirs go up, ours go up and when theirs come down, ours come down.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has indicated that what happens in the United States has an influence on what happens in Canada. Of course, that is the case. What else would one expect of a country with a branch plant economy which is closely intertwined with the economy of the United States? What would one expect of a country which is essentially a colony of the United States? What would one expect from a Liberal government and, I would add, from the Tory conti-nentalist approach to the economic systems within North America which is to see Canada and the United States as one, an approach which has essentially ignored the existence of the forty-ninth parallel? As a result of this continual progression toward a continentalist policy, and there is no indication that that is changing at all, we have had high interest rates that have chased those in the United States which are now likely to go to 2.0 per cent and above. This does not have to be the case. If we had an economy which was a Canadian economy, if we were in control, we would be more like Japan, West Germany or Switzerland. The interest rates in Japan are around 8.8 per cent, the interest rates in West Germany are around 11.5 per cent, in Switzerland they are about 5.7 per cent and in the United Kingdom they are in the 15 per cent area.
In other words, we do not have to have the high interest rates that obtain today in Canada. They are a reflection of the leaderless economy in Canada and its close ties to the United States. That is the reason that our prime rate today is 18.25 per cent. 1 suggest that the government's priorities in dealing with these problems are completely out of whack with reality. The government's main concentration of activity and interest is on the constitution, and yet when one travels across the country or to my riding of Kamloops-Shuswap and asks people what is foremost on their minds, what their major concerns are today, no one ever mentions that the constitution is their major concern. Their major concern is the cost of food, the cost of housing, the cost of travelling to and from work, whether their
December 19, 1980

children should go to college, and whether it is worth it as the future is so uncertain.
There is a frightened feeling out in the land. Those are the things that are on people's minds today, not whether or not the constitution should be patriated and whether or not it should have a certain kind of amending formula.
The people of Canada have received a great Christmas present from the government in 1980-an economic crisis, an economic catastrophe. If there is one sector of our economy that suffers dearly during these times, it is the small business sector, the sector which provides 50 per cent of the work force of Canada, the sector which provides essentially the new jobs that are being created today. The growing sector of our economy is the small business sector, not the branch plant sector. That is where the research and development is occurring, sometimes about 14 per cent of the value of sales in some of these small businesses. That is the sector that is exporting the finished goods and products from Canada to overseas markets. That is the creative, innovative sector-not the branch plant sector but the small business sector. That is where the creative instincts are played out. It is the sector of our business community which has a commitment to this country, which has a commitment to the communities in which it is found and to its neighbourhood. These are the firms that are providing assistance to the Little Leagues, and providing funds to allow the Boy Scout movements to exist.
This is the aspect of our economy that reflects the flavour of Canada, the personality of Canada. The Liberals and their policies are assassinating this sector, bringing it to its knees. They say they have lots of plans for the small business community, lots of schemes, lots of programs. Of 200 business programs in Canada, how many cater to the business sector? Two programs out of 200 are for the business sector, and those two are rather minimal. One is the Small Businesses Loans Act. The banks do not tell anybody about these programs. The small business development bond, because of its excluding clauses, makes it applicable to only 5 per cent of Canada's 940,000 small businesses. That is the kind of assistance that is available.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) has the gall to rise in the House of Commons and say, "We are studying the matter and we will study it for the next number of months." A businessman cannot meet a payroll with studies. He has to go to the banks and is forced to borrow at high interest rates. When a small entrepreneur or a contractor does a job for an individual, he often has to wait 30 or 60 days before he is paid. To meet his costs he has to go to the bank and borrow at today's interest rates, and that is 18.25 per cent, depending on the risk. That is the kind of support that is available to the small business sector.
Mr. Speaker. I see my time has run out. To conclude, 1 should like to quote from the Scriptures and say, "Lord forgive them for they know not what they do."

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate. I should like to express appreciation to my leader for initiating this debate on the economy and on the tragic failure of the government to act.
This debate is important for two reasons. First, it is important that we take every possible opportunity-no matter how small it is-to make the Liberal government face up to the consequences of its inactivity. This is a slender hope, but we must hold on to it. Perhaps we might wake the government up to the crisis we are facing. Second, if we fail to wake up the Liberals, at least we want to let Canadians know who is responsible.
Other speakers have already outlined the basic situation and the disastrous combination of factors which creates the present crisis. There is high unemployment. Over 853,000 people are officially unemployed, but when we add to that the number of people who have given up actively looking for work, we realize that the figure is actually 1.3 million people. Also, the Bank of Canada interest rates are the highest in our history. The rate announced yesterday was 17.63 per cent and today the prime interest rate is 18.25 per cent. As all members of the House know, most people must pay a much higher rate than that. We have also experienced the greatest increase in the cost of living in the last five years. Today, it costs people 11.2 per cent more to live than it did last year at this time. The price of food increased 13.7 per cent in November, 1980, over what it was in November, 1979. As the American poet, Randall Jarrell said, "It is a sad day at the supermarket".

Hon. members opposite should think about it- it is a sad day at the supermarket for the people of Canada. 1 should like to see the Liberal government do better than that. Housing starts are down 20 per cent from last year. This is at a time when most of our cities have a minus zero vacancy rate. Each of these conditions represents the failure of the Liberal government to keep its promises. But, when we take these conditions together, they constitute a massive betrayal of trust.
During this past week we watched the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicate his inability to do anything about the gathering crisis. It reminded me of some lines which were written by a Canadian socialist poet who was killed during World War II, Bertram Warr. His poem was entitled: "Working Class" and reads:
They have gashed the lands with cities
And gone away afraid when the wounds turned blue.
We are left with the politicians who think poorly of us And who stand back with chaos in their pale old eyes Whimpering, "That is not what we wanted.
No, it was not to have gone that way".
They are very old but we have been very ill And cannot yet send them away.

During the past week we have seen chaos in the eyes of the Minister of Finance, who whimpers and says, "This is not what we really wanted".
i should like to make a few remarks concerning the effect of this situation upon Indian people. During the past week the constitutional committee heard several Indian organizations talk about the threat to their survival as a people. Development projects and government policies have taken Indian people away from their traditional economy which has been based on the land. More and more Indian people today are being brought into a cash economy. But, too often they have been brought into a cash-economy situation without being given the means to obtain the cash, except as welfare recipients. We all know welfare does not keep up with inflation. Too often large-scale developments have not bothered to hire or train local Indians for all but the most casual jobs, those jobs where they are the last hired and the first fired. The government has not made sufficient money available to Indian bands for economic development, and what money is available requires so much by way of front end equity that the bands which need it most are least able to get it. In spite of inflation, funding to Indian bands has been frozen at the 1975 level. We expect Indian people to manage their affairs with 1975 dollars.

That is correct. Indian bands face a continuing problem with funds arriving late, so they are required to go to the banks to borrow money at exorbitant rates which cut into their very slender resources.
I should like to refer to some of the concerns of the people in my constituency. Last night as I was preparing for this debate, I phoned some of these people and asked them how the conditions affected them. First I spoke with a millworker who told me about some of his fellow workers who had to renegotiate their mortgages. From payments of $500 or $600 per month, their rates would be increased to $800 or $900 per month out of a take-home pay of $ 1,400, $ 1,500, or $ 1,600 per month.
This is not an isolated situation which affects just those people. We know that high interest rates mean no housing starts. Millworkers realize that when there are no housing starts, there are no lumber sales and so their jobs are threatened. The mill in which he works, like most mills in British Columbia, is stumbling along. It has no firm orders, but it is cutting lumber in the hope that markets will pick up in the spring. This Christmas, at the very time when workers are concerned that they are falling behind in some of their payments, most mills will be facing longer shutdowns than usual.
The anxiety of woodworkers is reflected in the fact that they are not making major purchases at this time of the year, such as refrigerators, sofas or stereos. We know the multiplying effect this has upon the economy. My friend pointed out that the classic system of free enterprise had completely disappeared; that many companies no longer dropped prices when sales were down; instead they raised prices to keep their profits up. This millworker wondered why it was that lumber sales were down, but profits were up.
I also talked with a small troll fisherman about the multiplier effect of what is happening. He pointed out that every fisherman is concerned about interest rates because he has to finance his operations for next year. In another three months he will be getting ready for the 1981 fishing season. High interest rates are especially difficult for fishermen who are making payments on their boats. Because of the intense ongoing gear war, fishermen have been required to equip their boats with more and more gear. They have found it necessary to borrow money in order to do that, and now they are in a real bind.
Not only does this affect fishermen, but it affects the small businessman who does business with them. I heard of the situation where one small or medium-sized supplier gave out lines of credit to several fishermen so that they could purchase gear. This is a normal procedure, but when these fishermen lost their boats because they were seized, the supplier was unable either to get his payment or to recover the gear. In this case there were seven boats affected just from one supplier.
The federal government has raised the licence fees by 100 per cent. The cost of diesel fuel has risen by one third. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, salmon fishermen on the Pacific coast face a very poor year. The catch is down by one-third, and on top of that the price of salmon has been down one-third. Many fishermen just do not know what their future is going to be; they fear that many boats will be forced out of the industry and they will not know until next season.
I talked with an elderly couple who were nearing retirement age and had their own modest home and grew a great deal of their own food in their own garden. They are beginning to look forward to receiving old age security, but they are not looking forward to it with any hope. They find the whole situation rather scary. They wonder what inflation is going to do to them once they are dependent on that pension. They are very close to the margin right now and the cost of food today hits them very hard. They ask why governments cannot do something. They ask, what is the possibility of currency controls? Who does it benefit, they ask, to keep the value of the dollar up? They certainly feel that it does not benefit them.
Then they ask whether the constitutional issue is simply a smokescreen to keep the people of Canada from focusing upon their real needs. For example, I talked to a butcher who was wondering what effect high interest rates would have upon his business. He asked how he could justify borrowing money to carry on business when he had to pay 19 per cent or 20 per cent to borrow that money. He is very much aware of the way in which cost of living increases affect people on fixed incomes. They are buying cheaper cuts and smaller amounts. He told me about some of his elderly customers who ask him to weigh a particular cut of meat. Then when he tells them how much it will cost, in many cases they have to say they are sorry, they cannot afford it, and they ask him to show them something less
December 19, 1980

expensive. He told me that it hurts him to do that, but he has to survive as well. His rent is going up. The cost of wrapping material has almost doubled over the last two and a half years and, of course, the wholesale price of beef has gone up.
Then I talked to a woman on unemployment insurance. She receives $81 per week unemployment insurance, or something like $330 per month. She has been listening to the debate and had heard Liberals say that everything was indexed. As far as she was concerned, any indexing was a sham. She said there was no way that it had risen along with the cost of living increase. She is making very high payments on oil and on hydro, since the previous summer while waiting for her unemployment insurance payments to come through she fell behind in meeting her payments. The Lord help the person who begins to fall behind in this society!
Her son is also out of work. She pointed to the fact that there were many families who have traditionally depended upon more than one wage earner, yet all of them are now out of work. She referred to the cynical statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to how people had to rearrange their priorities. She said that the only way you can do any rearranging is to cut down on how much you eat and skip buying clothes altogether.
The general impression I got from talking to these sorts of people, Mr. Speaker, was that they were uncertain and anxious. They were even living in fear of the future. They wanted to know where their problems were going to end. It is just not good enough for the Liberals to say that the members on this side of the House are spreading doom and gloom, because they themselves have already done that. The people already sense what we on this side of the House have been documenting for the last day and a half; they sense the frightening fact that there is no one in control.
All of the people 1 talked to felt the effects of high interest rates and the increased cost of living, but they are also able to point to other people who suffer even more from these effects. They were concerned that those least able to look after themselves were getting left behind. They do not want to go back to a dog eat dog society.

They have a sense that the Liberals are constantly dragging in the constitution in order to evade the real problems that confront the nation, that the constitution is only a smokescreen. If the constitution is only a smokescreen, then the people of Canada are beginning to see through it. Or, rather, the horrifying reality behind that smokescreen is beginning to appear.
I say to the members of this House that the unemployed woodworker on Vancouver Island has a great deal more in common with unemployed auto workers in Windsor than with any of the fat cats who talk about western separatism. Therefore, along with other members of my party I urge the government to take this crisis seriously and make themselves aware of the way it affects ordinary Canadians. We ask them to bring in a new budget in January which will provide some real relief and get the economy of Canada moving again. We ask them to bring in a fair prices commission with the power to roll back unfair price increases, and, finally, Mr. Speaker, we ask them to get working now on an industrial strategy which will put Canadians back to work, which will bring together the resources of this country and the skills of the people of this country, and thus create an economy which will be fit for the people of this country.
